speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEASURES TO COUNTERACT FOREIGN CONCESSIONAL FINANCING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members are aware, my department together with the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has been engaged over the past few months in a study of the impact on Canadian manufacturing interests of so-called concessional financing made available by some foreign governments on exports to Canada. This study has now been completed and I should like to make a statement concerning our findings and recommendations.
Most industrialized countries have been making export financing facilities available for many years. Until the recent sharp rise in the market rates of interest, government export financing was normally available at rates of interest equal to-if not higher than -the domestic lending rates. Government export financing was therefore not usually a factor influencing sales between the developed countries. It did play a useful role in financing sales to developing countries which-as is well known

lack capital and the ability to attract it on the required scale from conventional sources.
As is well known over the past two years domestic rates of interest have increased at a rapid rate throughout the world. Export financing, on the other hand, continues to be available in some countries at about the
same rates of interest as before. Coupled with the shortage of domestic funds, the availability of financing at favourable rates of interest has now become a significant factor in export sales between the developed countries, and this is where the problem lies.
In recent months, Canadian machinery manufacturers have been making representations to the government indicating that they are unable to sell machinery for projects in Canada because they cannot meet the highly attractive financing terms which are available to their foreign competitors. Moreover, Canadian manufacturers claim that because of the attractive credit terms available from abroad, they sometimes lost business-or were even denied the opportunity to bid-on projects which benefited from federal government assistance under the Area Development Incentives Act.

The government is satisfied that in several instances the availability to foreign manufacturers of export credit at lower rates of interest has resulted in substantial loss of business to individual Canadian companies which otherwise would have been competitive in price, performance and delivery.
There is also the danger that should export credit competition among the industrialized countries be permitted to continue, an increasing number of countries will resort to it and this may eventually develop into a full scale credit race. It is evident that credit competition of this magnitude can in the long run benefit no one.
In the light of these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, the government has decided to take a number of steps designed to mitigate the adverse impact of foreign government financing of exports to Canada which causes injury to Canadian industry.
First, Canada will use all available means consistent with its international obligations to curtail foreign government financing of exports to Canada in cases where it causes material injury to Canadian industry. In this context, consideration will be given to invoking the provisions of the Anti-Dumping Act in specific cases.

Second, we are pursuing the matter in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development-OECD-with a view to arriving at internationally agreed rules for the extension of government-assisted export credits between industrialized countries.
Third, in providing regional development incentives the Department of Regional Economic Expansion will take into consideration any adverse impact which foreign government export financing may have on Canadian industry. The regulations under the Regional Development Incentives Act already require that Canadian manufacturers shall be given an opportunity to supply machinery and equipment required for regional development projects, provided they can do so on terms which are competitive in price, delivery and performance.
Fourth, pending progress through international action, the Export Development Corporation will continue to match competitive financing offered by other countries to enable Canadian exporters who can compete in foreign markets to do so essentially on the basis of price, quality and delivery.
These measures should go some way in dealing with the immediate problem of injury to Canadian manufacturers. They should also provide a basis for an eventual long-term solution through international action.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEASURES TO COUNTERACT FOREIGN CONCESSIONAL FINANCING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad indeed that the government is now taking some steps to improve the competitive position of Canadian industry both in the domestic market and as far as exports are concerned. I regret that action along these lines, and further action which I will suggest, has not been taken prior to this time. I believe that the government has been derelict in its duty in that it did not perceive what was happening to the competitive position of our manufacturers particularly and of industry generally because of developments not only in regard to interest rates but also other impediments to the export of Canadian goods.
With regard to export financing, I hope there will not be a world-wide race in credit competition because, as the minister has stated, this will do no one any good in the long run. I hope all possible steps are being taken to see that world-wide credit competition does not develop.
The minister referred to a number of steps that the government intends to take. The first

was that consideration will be given to invoking the provisions of the Anti-Dumping Act in specific cases. I trust that in doing so the provisions of the new anti-dumping legislation enacted last year will not be interpreted according to the letter of the law, as some officials might be inclined to do. In other words, when any person feels he has been injured by the importation of goods there should be a pretty wide interpretation of what constitutes injury under the anti-dumping law. It should not be interpreted as strictly as it has been in the past, and possible or likely injury should be taken into consideration.
In addition to the use of the Anti-Dumping Act, I believe that the government should make use of the import-export control legislation which we have on our statute books. I know from personal experience that there has always been a considerable feeling among the departmental officials particularly that import controls should not be invoked. When I was minister of agriculture I invoked them on several occasions against the advice of the officials of the Departments of External Affairs, Trade and Commerce and so on. We did not, as a matter of fact, suffer any adverse effects from the imposition of import controls.
There is no question in my mind that import controls ought to be used under present world circumstances to a much greater extent than has been the case in the past, and I am thinking particularly of the difficulties of the Canadian electronics, footwear and textile industries. Imports coming into this country are destroying these industries and creating widespread unemployment. The government should be looking much more strongly than it has been at the means at its disposal, including import controls, to correct that situation.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEASURES TO COUNTERACT FOREIGN CONCESSIONAL FINANCING
speechtext: That is good Tory policy.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEASURES TO COUNTERACT FOREIGN CONCESSIONAL FINANCING
speechtext:
The second point the minister made is that in the organization for Economic Co-operation and Development an effort will be made to arrive at internationally agreed rules for the extension of government-assisted export credits between industrialized countries. Everything possible should be done along that line, but I think it should be realized that on the basis of past experience this is not a very well founded hope. We are looking for concrete results, but I believe we should not delude ourselves that we are likely to achieve very much through the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Develop-
May 26, 1970	COMMONS
ment. We must therefore rely on other means at our disposal, some of which I have already mentioned.
The third point relates to the supplying by Canadian industry of machinery and equipment for regional development projects. As is pointed out in the statement the minister made, Canadian manufacturers can do so provided they are competitive in price, delivery and performance. In my opinion, Canadian manufacturers ought to be given a preference in these projects which are financed with moneys provided by the Canadian taxpayer. In every other country that I know of local manufacturers are given a preference in government projects of this nature, and the same thing ought to apply in Canada.
The fourth point the minister made is that, pending progress through international action, the Export Development Corporation will continue to match credit financing offered by other countries. This is all to the good. I hope this course will be pursued very vigorously indeed, and that fear that we may lose a certain amount of money on a particular deal will not stand in the way of the Export Development Corporation being authorized to finance large numbers of these projects.
I end by saying that I hope the measures announced by the minister will be effective in improving our competitive position in both the domestic and export markets and that some of the other measures I have mentioned, particularly the imposition of import controls, will also be resorted to.

Mr. Speaker, I have raised the question of concessional financing with the minister on a number of occasions. I have waited for a statement from him for some time and have been optimistic about the kind of statement we might hear from the minister. I regret to say that the minister's statement is not the least bit convincing. As with so much the minister does and suggests, it lacks bite, it lacks any effective mechanism indicating our determination to take action.
There is much in the statement with which I can agree. The four motherhood clauses are great stuff. We are all in favour of co-operating with and talking to other countries in order to see what can be done. But the minister has left out of his statement one essential element which would have indicated that he meant business. I refer to the fact that members of industry strongly urged the immediate imposition of countervailing duties when it is 22375-45

It is time that the government got tough and showed some determination to act. Too often it has happened with regard to the automobile and textile industries, and it is now happening in regard to concessional financing, that there is a great wringing of hands and a great outpouring of intellect, but nowhere do we find any indication that this government means business. The government is quite willing to get tough with old age pensioners, but when it comes to getting tough with foreign countries capable of taking care of themselves they act like mice. This has to change and this is what I understand when I look at the statement the minister has just made.
It would be one thing if we were talking about an industry that is asking for protection or one that is not strong and competitive. The machinery industry has been placed at a disadvantage by what is going on, and it is among the most efficient and capable industries in our country. They are not asking for special concessions, nor should they be given special concessions. They are asking for the opportunity to bid against foreign countries on equal terms. As matters now stand, they are totally excluded from some bidding because of the financing that has been arranged by foreign countries. The financing is arranged first and when those companies accept the financing they must agree that Canadians will not be permitted to bid. This is an intolerable situation, particularly when it occurs in a designated area.
The industry of Ontario has never voiced any real objections to regional programs to assist the less-developed parts of Canada. As a matter of fact, they have reacted to the program with considerable enthusiasm. However, if this problem is not solved, if the tax money which they have contributed to assist the less-developed parts of Canada is going to be used to exclude them from bidding and to benefit foreign manufacturers only, I suggest to the government that they may jeopardize their entire program.
It is time we stopped being nice fellows because the kind of nice fellow this government has been is very little removed from being a patsy. It is time this government

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEASURES TO COUNTERACT FOREIGN CONCESSIONAL FINANCING
speechtext:
At first sight, Mr. Speaker, the four-part program announced today by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) appears hesitant and temporary. Canada has always been a loser in the international field.
Mr. Speaker, we must export to survive, but Canadian industry must also be protected if we are to do so.
The Canadian government therefore has two related, but no less important roles to play. What worries me is that the statement of the minister disregards altogether these two basic principles.
First of all, we must promote the development of Canadian industry, not only by taking into account the adverse impact of concessional financing offered by foreign governments, but also by encouraging, through appropriate and strict measures, greater consumption of Canadian products by Canadians.
Needless to say that the measures proposed today by the minister will prove clearly insufficient, mere palliatives, if he does not come up with practical and precise measures to encourage greater consumption of Canadian products.
It is true that we must export to survive, but it has never been said nor proven that export programs prevented on-the-spot or foreign consumption of Canadian products.
Canada is no exception to the rule and perhaps it is the most affected by exports. Indeed, Canadian labour costs more than in some other countries and, besides, the federal government has never adopted true measures to protect Canadian products against the competition of imported commodities.
In fact, the example of the shoe industry is enough to show the weakness of the four proposals of the minister. In 1967, when the population of Canada was only 20 million inhabitants, our country imported-as I say, imported-almost as much footwear from Asiatic countries or socialist countries as did all the countries of the Common Market, with a total population of 185 million.
During that period, that is from 1966 to 1970, the number of employees in the footwear industry in Canada has decreased from 25,360 to less than 21.000. Since January 1,


1970, an average of one footwear plant is closing down each week.
In addition in Canada, most women's and a few men's footwear plants are producing at less than 80 per cent of their normal capacity and more and more people are being laid off. As for imports and exports, it seems that the policy of this government is bringing about the destruction of the Canadian industry instead of supporting it.
So, I take this opportunity to point out to the minister the weakness of the inappropriate and temporary measures taken by the government. If he fails to take the necessary action, he will be among those responsible for the closing down of many drug or shoe manufacturing concerns in Canada, to the benefit of foreigners.
The Ralliement creditiste is asking for strict controls on imports to Canada and for the promotion of Canadian goods consumption in this country.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT INCLUDING RESEARCH AND PLANNING AND IMPLEMENTATION OF PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended speaking on Bill C-144, the Canada Water Act, because it seems that almost every Canadian is making some sort of representation on the subject. I felt I should abstain from contributing my own two cents' worth. However, after having listened to yesterday's debate, I felt impelled to speak and make one or two observations. It seems that pollution in Canada has become the concern of every mother's child and it seems that every mother's child in the cabinet wants his share of the mud pie. That seems to be the factor governing our anti-pollution legislation. Canada at present could be an international leader in pointing the way to methods for controlling pollution. During the last six weeks, however, I have been concerned at seeing the introduction of three pieces of legislation coming under the aegis of the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis), the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien), and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) which seek to control some aspects of pollution in Canada.
I am speaking to clause 8 of the bill and I feel very seriously that what we are doing now will establish a legislative precedent that will weaken Canada's ability to control pollution in this nation. I submit, therefore, that there is absolutely no need for Bill C-144, and, I will give my reasons for saying so as I go along. As a matter of fact, if the government is truly concerned about pollution, if it wishes to do Canada some great justice and to strengthen Canada's position in the fight against pollution, the best thing it could do would be to withdraw the bill altogether. Although I support the amendments put forward by my colleagues in the House, I wish to indicate in a preliminary way why I think the government ought to withdraw the bill altogether.
First of all, the government introduced Bill C-202 under the aegis of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the excuse being that we needed the legislation because there was no machinery under which to police pollution in our Arctic waters. These are the waters lying north of the sixtieth degree latitude, a line which runs through the
May 28, 1970

northern parts of the prairie provinces and the tip of Quebec and Labrador. The excuse is that we need the new legislation because the government lacks authority to enforce pollution measures in the area. The simple truth is that for 50 years the fisheries department of Canada has been armed with a special provision which allows it to police pollution in Arctic waters. The Department of Fisheries ought to be allowed to play an increasingly greater role in matters of pollution control; instead, the government is diminishing that department's responsibilities in this area.
I wonder how many hon. members have read Bill C-202? I will bet that there are very few in this House, and I include some of the ministers of the Crown in my remarks, who have looked at Bills C-202, C-204 and C-144, the three bills that deal with some aspects of pollution. All three bills contain similar definitions; they all have the same aims and objectives and, as the government hopes, they will bring about similar results. There, we have three pieces of legislation aimed at exactly the same things. Actually, the aims of these pieces of legislation are summarized in clause 8 of Bill C-144.
The very existence of Bill C-144 flies in the face of certain pollution control principles. I do not know what the professional term is; I am trying to say that there must be control from the top and not any dual control. Here, in this area, we are seeing a triplication of control, because three ministers are involved with pollution matters. Control will be quadrupled as soon as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) brings in amendments to the Transport Act. We will then see four captains in control of pollution, if I may use a phrase of the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse). Four captains will be in charge of the ship. Right now we have the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who is the senior captain, the Minister of Fisheries who ought to be, and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, all in charge of one ship. Not even the Manhattan could carry on under these conditions.
I understand that several provinces are challenging the constitutionality-that is a big word the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) uses these days-of Bill C-144. They say that it trespasses on their jurisdictional area as laid out at the time of Confederation in 1867. The Department of Fisheries was to have control over all waters, except those I suppose, that were so polluted there were no fish. There are
Water Resources Programs no waters in Canada-except a few-which have been polluted to the extent that no fish live in them and, therefore, there are no waters in Canada that do not come under the authority of the Department of Fisheries, so far as that authority relates to pollution. As I say, the constitutionality of the bill is being challenged. Many Canadians think as I do, that this piece of legislation is not a move in the right direction. The costs and powers involved are important factors to consider.
I see Mr. Speaker looking a little restless, no doubt because he thinks I am straying a little bit from the clause in question, clause 8 of Bill C-144. In order to clarify the point I wanted to make it was necessary for me to give some background information. We are considering clause 8, the penalty clause, which provides, if I may summarize, that no waste shall be deposited in any management area. In other words, once a management area has been designated, no waste may be deposited in that water under any circumstances, except with the permission of the management authority which will lay down certain limits for pollution.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Many people challenge the definition of "waste". I see that the minister is not listening to my remarks, but that is par for the course in Parliament and I am not worried about it. Perhaps someone is listening. The hon. member for South Shore is listening. Perhaps if I could get the minister's attention for one moment-I am referring to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who is sitting there on my left-I could tell him the word "waste" has a definite meaning which is not connected with pollution. I agree with the hon. member for South Shore that that word already has a legal definition. The hon. member has put that definition on the record. I support the argument of the hon. member for South Shore that if this bill is ever tested in court, it will not take a very smart lawyer to have it thrown out on the basis of the word "waste". This definition goes back as far as the history of navigation. Waste refers to a bunch of cloths or rags for cleaning an engine. That is the interpretation of the word "waste". Even though that may sound like a flimsy basis, I contend that that clause will not hold water if it ever gets in court.
The amendments introduced by the two hon. members pertain to the generality of the application of clause 8. As it is now defined, clause 8 can apply only to a very few circum-
May 26. 1970

Water Resources Programs stances. Clause 8 can only apply if a province agrees that a certain area should be a water management area. What do you do outside this area? If the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry were here he would say, don't worry because we now have Bill C-204 which is almost law. The Fisheries Act goes back to Confederation. It has been amended through the years and the present act actually had its origin in 1932, 38 years ago. At that time clause 3 of the Fisheries Act read and I quote:
"(2) No person shall cause or knowingly permit to pass into, or put or knowingly permit to be put, lime, chemical substances or drugs, poisonous matter, dead or decaying fish or remnants thereof, mill rubbish or sawdust or any other deleterious substance or thing, whether the same is of a like character to the substances named in this section or not, in any water frequented by fish, or that flows into such water, nor on ice over either such waters."
I will now paraphrase clause 3 of Bill C-204 because I was in committee when it was amended:- no person shall deposit or permit the deposit of any dilatory substance of any type in any water frequented by fish or in any place under any conditions where such dilatory substance or any other dilatory substance that results from the deposit of such dilatory substance may enter any such water. The word "waste" was changed all the way through. I am playing it by ear, that is putting in the changes as I read the definition.
This Fisheries Act has never been applied because there has never been a great deal of concern about pollution. If applied, Bill C-144 would be unnecessary. It is a waste of the Canadian taxpayers' money. It is a waste of time and energy, and there is no need for it. It is superseded by Bill C-204. I am aware that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources wants his share of the mudcake, and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development wants his cut of the pie. However, there is no way we in Parliament can act as school boys and take away the power of the Minister of Fisheries.
What will happen in case of a conflict? What will happen if the Minister of Fisheries is not satisfied with certain standards which permit certain effluent to pass into an area in which there are fish? Is that the end of it? Is the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources the czar who controls our anti-pollution measures or is the Minister of Fisheries? We have guaranteed that it will not be the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources because there is an amendment in this particular bill to the effect that this must be solved at the cabinet

level. That is not satisfactory because several ministers could be in conflict over who has control of the anti-pollution measures in this nation. I am losing the attention of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Perhaps I am polluting the atmosphere in the House. If so, perhaps I should be ruled out of order.
We now have a bill before us that has passed the second reading stage and the committee stage. It has been amended. It is a very powerful bill. There is really no need to amend the Fisheries Act because we have had the act as long as Parliament has existed, although1 it has not been enforced. This act provides penalties. It gives a tremendous amount of authority to the government to act in the event that pollution occurs. Perhaps it needed to be amended to bring it into line with the modem society in which we now live. The only problem with that act is that it has never been enforced.
I remember many incidents of pollution caused by firms, fish firms in particular, dumping their waste into the Atlantic Ocean. These firms were not prosecuted. They simply argued that it was a large body of water and therefore the problem was not serious. Canadians have become very concerned about pollution in the last five years. Canadians were aroused when they were informed of the pollution at Long Harbour in Newfoundland. This past week I had an opportunity, along with some of my colleagues, to fly over a sulphur plant in Long Harbour. It was an ugly sight. We were shown settling ponds into which effluent, which was once channelled into the ocean, is now being channelled. This eliminates a great danger. When that effluent was dumped into the ocean it not only destroyed millions of fish, but a way of life. A whole bay of fish were completely destroyed overnight. This aroused the ire of Canadians.
This was not only a problem for Newfoundland, but all of Canada. People all across Canada began to listen to stories about the situation. Television companies sent in crews to film the event. Divers and underwater crews filmed what was happening on the bottom. People were amazed because the effects of this one industry polluting one bay cropped up all over the place. All of a sudden everyone was excited. This subject of pollution needs to be one of Canada's top priorities. I am very concerned over the fact that the government does not want to give the Department of Fisheries the status it deserves. Consequently, many types of legis-
May 26, 1970

lation are being introduced. Every minister of the Crown, in one way or another, has a finger in the pollution pie. This is of great concern to Canadians. It is not enough to have the government and various ministers concerned, we need one major authority.
The hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau), the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) and the hon. member for South Shore have all made this argument. I do not think anyone can refute it. Naturally, every government department and various agencies have a role to play, but they must complement one major authority. This major authority must have a great deal of power and discretion to deal with the problem.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
I do not think we will get that in this present bill. I am appalled by clause 8. The Canadian people do not realize that in Bill C-144 Parliament is being asked to dilute the efforts of this country to fight pollution. I am sure all hon. members have read this bill. It is a fundamental piece of legislation. Hon. members must be concerned that this bill does not give the federal government any authority or power. The only power the bill contains is one to request the provinces if they will go along with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources in setting up a management authority. The bill does not have the power to lay down standards for any given area. Should it be decided, for example, that there is need for a water management authority in the Shuswap area, which I visited recently, the authority would have power to enforce its standards in that area only. What about the rest of the province? As I say, I do not believe the provinces will co-operate. In the second place, there is no need for them to co-operate, because provisional authority is already vested in the Minister of Fisheries; he has it constitutionally, he has it by precedent over the years, he has it in legislation in the shape of the Fisheries Act. He has this authority under the terms of Bill C-204. He can say: You will not be permitted to pollute; we shall not tolerate effluence having a toxicity above a certain level. This is an enviable authority. I doubt whether there is a minister in Canada with the authority possessed by the Minister of Fisheries. Why are we not using it?

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I shall not delay these proceedings for longer than a minute or two. I have not spoken in the House on this subject earlier. We have made our position clear on numerous occasions before the Committee on External Affairs, the Committee on Northern Development and the Fisheries Committee where we have thoroughly, conscientiously and responsibly analyzed the legislation concerned. My hon. friend from South Shore, who has been in the House far longer than I have, has gone into this bill in great detail. We believe the Minister of Fisheries should exercise the authority he has right now. I am concerned lest this bill dilute the authority which exists to make a real effort to combat pollution. This is too serious a matter to be fooled around with for political reasons. The minister was here earlier. I expect he will want his finger in the pie.
I will recognize the Minister of Fisheries as the authority in matters of pollution control. Even if the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources lays down standards in certain areas, he can be challenged by the Minister of Fisheries. If it is intended to go ahead with the bill we are considering, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources should be given broad powers to ensure that the application of controls will extend right across Canada. It is not enough that it should apply only to areas with respect to which some sort of agreement has been reached. Failing this, it might be just as well to throw the bill out altogether. Perhaps the minister himself realizes there is no need for this legislation; maybe the intention is to continue in a make-believe fashion for a while until, eventually, when everyone realizes that the bill has no value, it will be recognized that the power should be placed where it belongs and where it can be exercises, that is to say, with the Minister of Fisheries.

speechtext:
It was
interesting to listen to the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan). His speech covered a wide range. I agree that these are worth-while amendments and that they would add a strength to the bill which is lacking at the present time.
Putting in fees as a deterrent has not worked in the United States or in Europe and
May 26, 1970

Water Resources Programs I do not believe it has worked, or will work, here. Members of my party are sceptical about these things. I am thinking of a pollution fee or deterrent which was put into the legislation in Ontario. K.V.P. had a mill, in Espanola and were dumping in a large amount of pollution-they were better at pollution than anyone in the Province of Ontario; they dumped everything and sundry into the water system of that area to the extent that the Water Commission had a look at it, and then, finding there were some influential people involved, decided not to do anything about it.
The people in the area took the K.V.P. to court. But before the court decision could be implemented in accordance with legislation in force in the Province of Ontario, the premier of the day, Leslie Frost, rushed a new bill into the Ontario legislature. This bill said, in effect, that in this particular area K.V.P. would be allowed to dump any waste they wanted into the water, as an exception. Of course, the company continued to do so. When changes were eventually made in the Ontario water control legislation the people again took the company to court. In one instance, the company was fined. The company had, of course, pleaded guilty. A fine of some $1,000 was imposed and the company was given a specific time in which to instal pollution control equipment. Naturally, the company did not do this and again the people of the area took the company to court. Once more there was a decision in favour of the people who had taken the action, and once more the company did nothing about it. This resulted in a $4,000 charge but to the best of my knowledge there has yet to be pollution control equipment installed, though I understand the company has been sold. This is an indication that it is cheaper to pay the fee than to instal the controls needed to stop pollution. The company found that a fee of $1,000, or even $4,000, was of no importance at all. It preferred to plead guilty and satisfy this small charge, or pay this licence.
It reminds me of the days when there was a great deal of bootlegging in some municipalities and the bottleggers expected every month or two months to be brought before the court and fined. This was exactly the same thing, in practice, as a licence. If the fine was not too heavy, your operation was obviously warranted for another month or two. When your turn came to be in court again you paid another fee and it just became a licensing fee. This happened in my constituency on a number of 
occasions. Everybody laughs about the licensing of bootleggers. Not everybody gets knocked off at the same time; it is done on a nice, friendly basis, in rotation. I presume they keep track of who got rapped last time and how long it is since somebody was asked to pay his licence fees in this way. This got around the Ontario liquor licensing regulations and it brought to the municipality the fees which it would normally expect to obtain if it were doing the licensing.
The same is true in connection with pollution. Many of the pulp and paper companies, in particular, have found it more profitable to operate on the basis of a fee or a fine than on the basis of a licence. I say we shall have to make up our minds whether we really want to stop pollution or not. Although the minister of fisheries announces in the House that fishing in Lake Erie, or in Lac St. Pierre, or in the Saguenay-in fact, in many parts of eastern Canada-has been ordered discontinued because of mercury pollution, he never tells the House that the plant responsible for the pollution has been closed. Again, this seems to me to be a sort of bootlegging operation. The government's approach is not one of: "Let's not put mercury into the water". Perhaps that would be too logical and too direct. Instead, the government announces that a certain stretch of water has been polluted by mercury, and as a result people will not be allowed to fish in it, that if they do they will die from poisoning.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
The government has also said that companies guilty of pollution can be taken to a civil court, and if blame can be proved to be directly attributable to the company, compensation may be had. But once again the government does not order the company not to pump mercury into the water. It seems to me that the pollution clauses in the bill are oriented to that sort of approach, which surely must be wrong. I am pleased to see the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Jerome) in the House today because I travelled through the Sudbury area, through "blizzard valley", for years and remember seeing the potato crops and field crops blighted. At one time you could not grow grass or clover in Sudbury, or even a shade tree.
If there is talk that International Nickel or Falconbridge may be forced to instal pollution control devices on their smoke stacks, the old bugaboo is always raised that the company will shut down and go out of business,
May 26, 1970

that they will close down the smelter and throw all the employees out of work. People have been scared and, as a result, nothing has been done about pollution control of this sort. Many years later along comes the government of Ontario and invests money in the establishment of secondary industry in the area. International Nickel is now manufacturing sulphuric acid and making a handsome profit from the operation. My point is that it is of advantage to industry to stop polluting the environment and to turn its endeavours toward other pursuits.
There are many immigrants in my part of Ontario and I remember recently talking to someone from the Ukraine, or Roumania, or Czechoslovakia, or Poland, I forget precisely which, about a river in his country flanked on either side by communities that collectively had a population which ran into millions. He was pointing out to me that the difference between the North American economy and the European economy is that, no matter the commodity, there was always a use for it in Europe. Waste just was not dumped into rivers. For example, he told me that when he was a young lad he used to swim in this river and drink the water from it. Although there were millions of people along its banks, the river was not polluted. There are very few people living along some of the rivers in northern Ontario, yet they are badly polluted. Although the people have been few, the pollution has been abundant. As this person pointed out, in Europe every commodity is worth something.
The sulphuric acid fumes emitted by the smoke stacks at Sudbury are not an asset but an immense liability to everyone living in the community as well as to all other industry in the area. They eliminate agriculture, destroy trees in the area and have a deleterious effect on community life. If you go to Sudbury today, Mr. Speaker, you will find grass and trees. In Sudbury there are five lakes, most of which are now used for recreational purposes. Previously they were dumps for mining waste. I am sure that if industrial waste were analysed it could be put to use in the building of secondary industry, industry that in some cases might produce a product even more valuable than the original product.
I remember as a boy going to Cobalt and seeing dozens of mines that had very large waste dumps. At the outbreak of war cobalt was in demand as a strategic war material. These mining dumps were picked over and the cobalt that had been found uneconomic to
Water Resources Programs process was used in the war effort. The cobalt came from the silver mines. The mining operation in those days was so primitive that one of the byproducts was also arsenic. During the war silver was not a commodity of major importance and many mines closed down, but due to the demand for cobalt some opened up again and mined what had hitherto been a waste product. In fact, cobalt proved a more valuable product than the mining of silver, which had been the original product of the mine. Therefore, I suggest that if waste in North America is properly handled it need not be considered as waste. I am sure it can be proven that almost all types of industrial waste can serve some purpose and be put to good use. If the government would refuse to permit the dumping of industrial waste, I am sure some good use could be found for it on which, perhaps, totally new industries could be based.
Under the terms of the bill the government is not providing any money for research into sanitation control, an obvious field in which assistance is required. The bill indicates that assistance will be provided by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in sanitation control, which I presume means that the municipalities will be required to build proper sewage treatment plants.
In my own home town the municipality, with assistance I presume from the federal or provincial government, built a sewage disposal system and a lagoon. This reminds me of the story of some U.S. tourists who visited the town and decided to picnic on the shores of this nice looking lake with grass banks. There were not too many people around at the time and they decided to have a swim. Finally, someone from the sanitation department chased them away, telling them it was the sewage disposal lagoon of the municipality. That may be a very nice story, but in northern Ontario bacteria is not exposed to strong sunlight for as many months in the year as other parts of Canada, and the discharge from the lagoon into the river may be as pure as it is claimed to be. Eut it sure doesn't smell pure, as they say it should, and certainly it is not the kind of lagoon in which one would want to swim. Not even ducks are foolish enough to swim in it.
So, before these foolish controls are implemented, I suggest research should be done into whether or not the expenditures that the municipalities will be required to make will provide satisfactory pollution control in the
May 26, 1970

Water Resources Programs end. The federal government will have to take some responsibility for providing research into the type of controls that are possible. The municipalities are facing a financial problem in this connection. If they are going to be allowed, as I hope they are, to participate in the development of water management areas, I suggest the federal government will have to assume some of the burden of the cost.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
If the federal government does have a costsharing program for the maintenance of the management areas, then of course they will have some control through the withholding of their share of the grants to the municipalities until the necessary standards are met. If this is done, the federal government will have some say about the type of plant that will be allowed to locate in such an area and the type of waste control which will be implemented. I think that this method for the control of the management area will certainly be an improvement over the payment of fees.
I believe that greater co-operation in this area among municipal, provincial and federal governments, apart from matters involving constitutional issues, can be achieved, as it has been in other areas, through cost sharing programs in which the federal government through withholding its contribution can have some say regarding the development of the program. We have had good success in our cost sharing program for the construction of the Trans-Canada highway which had to be built to specifications before grants could be obtained. The province of Quebec decided to withhold its participation in the project, but eventually when money was made available for the construction of roads even the province of Quebec decided to meet those standards. We have now been able to develop universal standards across our nation and this has been to everyone's advantage.
This is true even in such mundane fields as education in which the government is not involved directly. We have been able, through cost sharing programs, to develop vocational education through the payment of construction and equipment grants that has ensured a standard of facility for all people.
I suggest that this may be one of the ways of assisting municipalities to participate in the implementation of this legislation and thus achieve uniformity. I suggest that the implementation of this legislation can be improved by the amendments before us. I do

not think it matters which amendment is accepted. Both have a similar purpose in view. But I suggest that by its refusal to consider these grants the government, the minister and his assistants are indicating that they have no understanding of the intent of the amendments or of the legislation which they put forward. It has become all too evident to everyone that the legislation before the House is not necessarily the legislation of the minister, of the cabinet or of the government but rather legislation drafted by civil servants who are not really in a position to provide the minister with sufficient information regarding the purpose of the bill to allow him to make a decision on the amendments. Sooner or later this will become known to the public, and they will become incensed at the inability and inflexibility of a government that cannot accept logical and advantageous amendments, the purpose of which is to make this legislation more realistic and meaningful to Canadians in general.
Pollution is only a word unless we are able to translate that word into legislation which will have an effect on the environment of Canadians. It seems to me that the amendment before us now will make this legislation more meaningful. I am sorry that the minister and the government are not capable of making a favourable decision on the amendment and that the vote, when it is taken, will only reflect the number of seats which the Liberal party holds rather than the merits of the amendments presented by the opposition.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. J. Orange (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT INCLUDING RESEARCH AND PLANNING AND IMPLEMENTATION OF PROGRAMS
speechtext:
In dealing with the two amendments before us I would like to start first with motion No. 8 in the name of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) which reads:
No person shall deposit or permit the deposit of waste In any waters.
To anyone who has read this amendment and who understands the process of the deposit of waste, the impracticability of the amendment is evident. It would mean, for example, that anyone throwing a cigarette package in a river would be depositing waste in our waters. It would mean also that people who are living in cottages along the rivers and lakes of our country would be immediately required to install septic tank systems- not that this is an undesirable requirement, but the impracticability of a proposal of this nature is such that I cannot see how it could be part of the Canada Water Act.
May 26, 1970

I believe that much the same reasoning applies to motion No. 9. For example, there is no substance known to man which in some way is not detrimental to man, animal, fish or plant. For example, the secondary or even tertiary treatment of wash water would not remove it from this particular definition of waste. Motion No. 9 would prohibit the deposit of these treated substances. I ask: just how do we propose to live in a world under these circumstances? Where would the effluent from our waste treatment plants go? The government's proposal is to classify all substances that are potentially detrimental, including water carrying such substances as waste, and then to control the deposit of these wastes by specifying how they must be treated, in what quantities and in what manner they can be deposited. To do otherwise is to ignore the Newton's basic law of physics that matter cannot be destroyed. This House and every physical thing will eventually end up as waste to be transported by the rivers to the sea. No law of man can change this.
What we can do, and what we intend to do under this act, is to regulate and control the manner and condition under which these wastes must be deposited. I suggest that this particular amendment ignores reality. There are very few substances that are not in some way detrimental to man, animal, fish or plant. To say that all other substances must be disposed of on land or in the air is really something that is impossible. We should recognize that water is often used as a proper disposal area as an alternative to air or soil, and that the treatment of the wastes going into it, so that they do not affect our environment or ecology, is the proposal put forward under the Canada Water Act.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I recognize, as do other hon. members on this side, the concern that many hon. members have with respect to control of waste. The hon. member who just sat down justified the need to have effective control over waste. I suggest to him, when he says that under this bill there is no money for research, that he is not quite accurate, particularly in view of the fact that at present under the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources comes the Canada Centre for Inland Waters, the Bedford Institute, and a number of other establishments which are either in being or are proposed to undertake research with respect to the quality and management of our water. The amendments, as proposed, do not meet

Water Resources Programs the basic requirements of the Canada Water Act, and I see no way that they can fit within the concept that has been advanced by the government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think anyone could be impressed by the argumentation of the Parliamentary Secretary, and I am very disappointed that the minister has not spoken. Both the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) and the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) have made it clear that they have no pride of authorship in motions Nos. 8 and 9, and if the minister thinks that the language of the amendments can be improved, they would be delighted to have him or his officials do so. Therefore, to make a picayune point about the wording of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Greenwood, saying it means that anyone who throws an empty cigarette package into the water will be violating the act, is merely high school debate rather than dealing with the substance of the question before us. Even if the minister disagrees with the positions we have taken, he owes it to Parliament and to the people of Canada to explain his disagreement. I hope he will do so, and will not merely sit at his desk listening.
There are two objectionable features with respect to clause 8, and the minister ought to rise to his feet, whenever he thinks it appropriate, to tell us we are wrong and the reasons why we are wrong. The first is a very profound problem, namely, whether or not clause 8 as presently worded has doubtful constitutional validity. I suggest to the House, as the hon. member for Greenwood did in great and learned detail, and as the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka did, that one does not have to be absolutely convinced that clause 8 is in difficulty. It should be sufficient that a doubt has been raised for the minister and the government to want to do something about it rather than spend the next few years in litigation in the courts.
Even if the government of the province of Ontario says it will not delay the implementation of this legislation by going to court, that will not prevent a private corporation that feels aggrieved from trying to take advantage of the question if its legal advice is that clause 8 as presently worded is of doubtful constitutional validity. That is not going to prevent any private corporation from hauling the legislation into court. I am not a constitutional expert. I cannot claim to have the
May 26. 1970

Water Resources Programs experience in constitutional matters that others have had, and that to my knowledge the hon. member for Greenwood has had. But I have had a little experience and I have certainly studied constitutional law. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the case which the hon. member for Greenwood made is a pretty strong and convincing case, not necessarily that the clause is unconstitutional, because no one can be definite about that except the highest court of the land, but that the present wording of the clause makes it of very doubtful constitutional validity and opens it up to possibly successful attack.
It is a well established principle in the interpretation of our constitution that if the federal Parliament seeks to regulate any activity that is within a sphere normally under provincial jurisdiction, then the Parliament of Canada is going beyond its powers. This is what clause 8 does. It talks about prescribing the quantities and conditions with respect to waste disposal in certain water quality management areas. That is surely nothing else except regulation, and if it is done in waters which are under provincial jurisdiction, and with respect to activities which are under provincial jurisdiction, then clearly there is justifiable doubt as to whether the Parliament of Canada has the authority under the B.N.A. Act to pass such legislation. That is the first objection to the clause. The hon. member for Greenwood and the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka in their amendments are in effect saying to Parliament, "Why get yourself into this morass of constitutional argument"?
May I remind the Parliamentary Secretary that waste is defined in the bill. No one is talking about waste as you, Mr. Speaker, or I might define it, such as an empty cigarette package. I doubt very much if that is waste defined in the bill. We are talking about waste as defined in the bill which is a "substance that, if added to any waters, would degrade or alter or form part of a process of degradation or alteration of the quality of those waters..."
What these amendments before the House say is that instead of getting into the questionable area of regulation, instead of getting into the morass of constitutional argument with the provinces, and possibly constitutional litigation in the courts, why not have the courage the situation demands to say simply that certain things are prohibited. This course would be clearly within federal jurisdiction because you would then be dealing with and enacting criminal law?


As I said the other day on another amendment, I cannot understand the minister's position on any of these things. He has not explained it. I hope he will. I have read his explanation on one other matter dealing with quality standards and I am darned, Mr. Speaker, if that came anywhere near an explanation. In fact, I doubt if the minister came anywhere near dealing with the subject, let alone explaining his position. I hope he will do better than that in this case.
I do not want to take too long because the area has been covered by the hon. member for Greenwood who gave a very full analysis of the legal problem involved. But I repeat to the minister: why do you need this? Why cannot you simply prohibit certain interference with water quality and thereby come clearly within federal jurisdiction, because you would then be dealing with criminal law? The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) will correct me if I am wrong but I believe he said that if anybody wants to change his language or his words he has no objection. He is not saying these are the best words, so it is not a question of the minister having to accept them. If he is willing to accept the idea, we would all be willing to stand this clause until he can communicate with his officials and come forward with an amendment which, in his view, better meets the situation.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
That is the legal objection to it but there is also a basic objection of principle. I cannot understand why the minister is making ringing speeches against pollution saying that the polluter must pay, talking about the need for cleaning our waters and then providing in this, the main act for dealing with water pollution, for an effluent discharge fee prescribed by the government. Under what circumstances? I challenge the minister to tell this House what it is he foresees. What kind of situation, what kind of condition does he foresee which would justify people being allowed to dispose of waste in a water quality management area on payment of the fee? What circumstances can justify this?
I draw your attention to the fact, Mr. Speaker, that this bill does not deal with all qualities of water. This clause deals with water quality management areas designated pursuant to certain clauses of the bill. If certain waters are designated a water quality management area and standards are set for the cleaning and the maintenance of them as
May 26, 1970

clean waters, I would like to know under what conditions anyone is entitled to pay a fee to pollute waters so designated. What has the minister or the government in mind?
What nonsense it makes of the minister's protestations about water pollution when he puts such provisions into the act. Individuals like yourself and myself are not involved, Mr. Speaker. What we have are corporate polluters, either large corporations, large industries or large municipalities, without the necessary equipment in some cases. In practice, they are the ones who are mostly responsible for the pollution. What situation, what condition, what kind of industry, what sort of quality has the minister in mind when he says that he is going to establish an effluent discharge fee? I suggest to the minister that those of us in this House who have the courage to challenge him to explain this outrageous situation are doing him, as well as the people of Canada, a service. I suggest to him that if the people around him, the members of his party, were expressing what every Canadian would want them to express they would ask these questions of him just as sharply as we are doing. Unless, of course, Mr. Speaker, they did so in some private caucus which I was quite happily unable to attend.
I ask the minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, why do you want an effluent discharge fee? Under what conditions are you going to permit an industry to pollute our waters as long as it pays a fee? Why should Parliament empower you to make regulations of this sort? We want to know if this fee is to be uniform right across Canada or if it will be possible for every agency, as defined in this act, to set its own effluent fee. If every agency is allowed to set its own effluent fee, as I think is contemplated here, then we will have competition between one area of the country and another as industry will realize it is possible to pollute some waters for a lower fee than others.
This opens the door, Mr. Speaker, to the possibility of destroying any effectiveness this bill might have. These are the two reasons for our objection to clause 8 and are the reason the amendments are before the House.
I am not asking the minister to get to his feet if he does not want to, but I say that he owes it to Parliament and to the people of Canada to explain, (a) why he is taking a risk on the constitutionality of this bill in clause 8, which is the heart of the enforcement provisions, and, (b) why he has asked Parliament to provide for an effluent discharge fee. In
Water Resources Programs other words, why is he providing for a fee which gives industry the right to pollute or to continue polluting. Why in Heaven's name is he doing these two things? Until he explains them to the satisfaction of this House the clause ought not to pass.

Mr. Speaker, Motions No. 10, 12 and 13 go together. They permit loans to be made to water management agencies for capital works. When the bill was originally introduced, this was one of the areas which still had not been completely covered. We discussed this matter at great length during the committee hearings and amendments were presented to the committee at that time regarding the question of capital loans. It had been our hope that possibly this matter could have been dealt with in committee; however, we were given to understand by the legal authorities that the matter should be brought up by way of amendment at the report stage in the House of Commons.
Our concept since the inception of the bill has been that the polluter must pay by service charges and effluent fees; but we also want to ensure that water treatment facilities are built as quickly as possible. Both goals can be achieved if we are permitted, under the bill, to make loans directly to the agencies. The loans would be paid off by service charges and fees, thus placing the financial burden where it should be, on those who deposit waste.
Motion No. 12 would permit the water quality management agencies to borrow from federal and provincial governments for capital works, and not necessarily from one level or the other by itself. Motion No. 13, as a consequence of Motion No. 12, provides that the amounts borrowed by the agencies for capital works shall be deposited with a chartered bank. As I indicated, during the course of our committee hearings there was extensive discussion on this matter by the committee members, and there seemed to be agreement that the motions we are proposing now

would carry without a great deal of discussion. That principle met with the general approval of all committee members.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the three motions before us now incorporate in part some of the suggestions I made during the second reading stage of the bill. However, they do not go as far as I would wish. I should like to see the bill contain financial commitments by way of contributions to the capital cost of projects undertaken under the Canada Water Act. However, the government has moved slightly by introducing loans for capital costs of projects, and I think this is good. We shall have no objection to that. We do not object to these three motions being passed together.
We must recognize that even though the minister has repeatedly said that the polluter must pay, a concept with which we agree in the main, there is much pollution in this country that cannot be attributed to any particular individual, municipal unit or factory. The concept that the polluter must pay envisions being able to identify the polluter. But if you cannot identify him, surely, there must be some government contribution or intervention in order to make sure the pollution is cleared up. These motions move in that direction, in that there will be loans with respect to capital costs of projects which clear up pollution, and to that extent I support the three motions being passed together.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT INCLUDING RESEARCH AND PLANNING AND IMPLEMENTATION OF PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the three motions we are discussing now will not be opposed by our party. We feel that they certainly improve the bill. We would not want the minister, his department or the government to feel that we are completely satisfied with the financial arrangements set out in the bill because, basically, the government has moved the burden of the cost of pollution to the provinces and municipalities. The Parliamentary Secretary said that those who pollute our waterways will have to pay the cost of cleaning them. I raise the point that we raised when debating the preceding motions. Why should people be allowed to pollute our waterways? That just shows you how stupid these provisions are. We ought not to have to collect effluent fees; we ought not to allow industry to pay money to pollute the waters which the citizens of this country must use.
I wish to make another point. The Parliamentary Secretary said that the polluter in the water quality management areas that must be set up must pay. I ask, what will
DEBATES	7343
Water Resources Programs happen in those parts of Canada in which no water quality management areas will be set up? Since there are no fees for those areas, will people be able to pollute with impunity? The Parliamentary Secretary and the minister are aware of this fact. What is going to be done outside the water quality management areas? We have been trying to get national standards established, and national enforcement, so that no one from one end of Canada to the other can pollute any of our waters. We fought through the various committee stages the need for some major changes as far as financing is concerned. These three amendments have made some small measure of change. We welcome these changes.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I wish to say a few words about the overall financial picture because these amendments deal with federal loans and grants. One of the main problems facing this nation is the fact that there is not enough money available to municipalities for the building of sewage treatment plants. Last year, $50 million was available through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This money ran out. There were dozens of applications from municipalities that did not have the money to lay on the line. They could not get grants to build the treatment plants which are needed to clean up a very sore spot as far as pollution is concerned. This year we are told an additional $25 million will be available.
I wish to put on the record one or two facts that I think the Canadian people should know. Sewage is one of the minor pollutants in Canada when compared to industrial pollution. A group representing the mayors and municipalities of Canada visited our committee. The cost of separating the storm sewers from the sanitary sewers in the city of Winnipeg, one of the first jobs they must do, will be $250 million. It will cost a quarter of a billion dollars just to separate the storm sewers from the sanitary sewers, and yet even after the expenditure of this amount not one treatment plant will have been built.
In the city of Toronto, a major portion of this sewer separation work has been carried out. It will cost an additional $200 million to split the balance of the storm sewers from the sanitary sewers before the job of building treatment plants can be undertaken. Practically none of the sewage in the city of Montreal is treated. The problem is the lack of funds for primary, secondary and tertiary treatment plants. These will cost hundreds of millions of dollars. It is going to cost billions
May 26, 1970

Water Resources Programs of municipal dollars to tackle the problem of sewage. There is no provision in this bill to give hope for the solution of this aspect of the pollution problem which is facing Canadians. The government has not done a good job as far as the over-all financial aspects of this pollution problem are concerned. We are justifiably worried that this one phase of the financial aspect, the cost of the treatment of sewage, is going to be loaded primarily on the municipalities and provinces.
The $75 million available through CMHC this year will not go anywhere. There is now a backlog of projects that will more than eat up the money which the government hopes to provide through CMHC. I bring this to the attention of hon. members in the hope that something will be done. The minister has talked of loans. More loans will be available for projects within these water quality management areas. However, as the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) pointed out yesterday, it will take a couple of years before we have any water quality management areas set up in Canada to which loans could be made to start the process of water management. It makes one wonder why when we are dealing with pollution on a national basis, this bill is so narrow in scope. All it is going to do is tackle these small water quality management areas provided for in the bill. We have gone over this before.
A little later on we will have an opportunity to speak about finances. I felt that I should put these remarks on the record and indicate that, while we are going along with these measures, we are not at all satisfied with the way this government, this minister and his department are attacking the over-all pollution problems facing the Canadian nation.
