(11) That Bill C-144, to provide for the management of the water resources of Canada including research and the planning and implementation of programs relating to the conservation, development and utilization of water resources be amended by striking out lines 22 to 25, both inclusive, page 16 thereof, and substituting therefor in clause 13(3) "(c) undertake the collection of effluent discharge for fees prescribed to be payable by any person for the deposit of waste in those waters [Mr. Harding.)
but in no case shall an effluent discharge fee be collected for the deposit of waste in respect of any project commenced after the establishment of the agency."
He said: Mr. Speaker, I consider that this amendment is the most important one before the House. We all claim some pride of authorship for our amendments, but the proposal in this particular amendment is fundamental to the elimination of pollution in Canada. If we do not accept it, we do not accept our responsibility to the people of Canada. I call this amendment the factory fence amendment. The reason I call it that is that the proposal, if accepted, would require all new installations after the passage of this act, whether they be industrial, municipal or private, to contain their waste within the limits of their own property and not to dump it into the public waters of Canada. It is as simple as that.
In this particular bill, we have a system of effluent discharge fees. We in the opposition, and I speak for both major parties which have taken part in this debate, have objected consistently to the effluent discharge fee as a system. However, the minister says no, it is fundamental to the bill. The minister says it is necessary to include these effluent discharge fees and that is what will be done.
There were some amendments rejected in committee. We understand they will be rejected again. We must be realistic in this debate. The minister is not going to accept the elimination of effluent discharge fees. I am proposing that if any company, municipality or individual is now allowed to dump waste in private waters and pay for it, that they should not be allowed to do so after this bill comes into effect.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT INCLUDING RESEARCH AND PLANNING AND IMPLEMENTATION OF PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT INCLUDING RESEARCH AND PLANNING AND IMPLEMENTATION OF PROGRAMS
speechtext:
We cannot do too much to clean up the pollution which is now being caused by dumping effluents into Canadian waters. We have to accept the system which is being proposed. We cannot say next week or next month when this bill is put into effect that no more waste water shall contain any pollutant. It would be an impossible request. So, the government has set up provision for water management agencies through whose efforts the pollution now being caused can be contained and the effluents treated to the best ability of the agency. All right. We accept this. But we are not ready to accept that any company has a right, after this bill comes into
May 26. 1970

force, to dump effluents from a new plant into the water. The amendment says that in no case shall an effluent discharge fee be collected for the deposit of waste in respect of any project commenced after the establishment of the agency. We have to take a stand somewhere. When do we start? I believe we ought to start now.
It is no use saying we are suffering from pollution now and that it will have to continue. There must be a cut-off point, and I say that the cut-off point for the continued dumping outside the factory fence is now. For too long this country has permitted waste and effluents to enter its waters. This bill is intended, I suppose, to make a start, if only a feeble start, toward controlling the situation. We should certainly not use the agencies which are to be set up in such a way as to permit the continuance of the dumping of effluent into public waters.
I have some support for my amendment from another minister of the government, the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis). I wish to read what he said in an address to the 25th Annual Meeting of the Fisheries Council of Canada in St. John's, Newfoundland, as summarized in the Montreal Gazette. These words are attributed to the minister, and he appears to be the author of this article. It reads:
Our message, essentially, is that pollution must be stopped at the factory fence. Harmful substances must be confined to the mill or the plant. Often large settling ponds have to be installed. The supernatant liquids from these ponds then have to be recycled back into the mill or the plant in question. Sometimes it costs millions of dollars to close these systems-but closed they must be!
Time never stands still. Technology is on the march. New chemical processes are introduced and new products put on the market. We must be, forever, on the alert. We must be on the lookout for new substances which can poison our environment.
We must be on the alert for new pollutants, especially those which can damage man himself.
That is the end of the quotation. It is my theory that the only way to clear up pollution in this country, and indeed throughout the world, is by recycling waste products. Recycling is the whole answer. Factories which are dumping waste must develop means of disposing of their waste products within their own premises. It can be done. To my knowledge most of the new factories in Ontario, the province in which I reside and in which I am particularly interested, are obliged to satisfy the Ontario Water Resources Commission that they will not be discharging effluents into the

Water Resources Programs water. Until their engineering has been perfected, permission to build a new plant is withheld. It is as simple as that. I have been involved with three or four plants which have been established in the area I represent. In each case, before the engineering had been completed, the Water Resources Commission representatives looked over the plant. They asked: "What are you going to do about your effluents?" The companies had to say: "We intend to instal settling ponds which will receive these effluents. We intend to dump water back in minimal quantities and that water will be pure, in fact, it will be purer than when we took it in." This has to be done. It has been done already in one province.
What will the situation be if the minister's water management agencies permit pollution on the payment of a fee and the Water Resources Commission of Ontario declines to do so? Who will win the battle. I hope it will be the Water Resources Commission of Ontario. I would hate to think that the rules the commission has set for new plants could be circumvented in accordance with the terms of this bill, and that new factories could once more discharge effluents and wastes on the payment of a fee. I hope this violent conflict will never arise, but it will if we pass this bill in its present form. I have mentioned Ontario specifically, but there are other provinces which are applying restrictions with different degrees of severity.
We ought to make a stand now. We cannot go on telling ourselves that some time in the future we intend to take action. Our environment is too badly damaged already. One thing we must do is improve the prospects for the future. Surely, that is why we are considering this bill right now. This is what we all believed the Canada Water Act was intended to do.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
If pollution is not stopped now, it will never come to an end. No matter how hard I try, I can think of no reason for not accepting this amendment. There is already in existence a pollution problem, and under the water quality management agencies that are to be set up plants that have been in existence for 50 years and which employ 300 or 400 people will gradually have to cut back on pollution. What pollution is discharged will be disposed of within our resources.
If this is the intention of the act, namely to deal with the pollution that exists now, then we will have to accept it and I only hope the
May 26. 1970

Water Resources Programs legislation will be effective. But I cannot accept this approach for the future control of pollution. I cannot accept any interference with the good pollution control work now being done in several provinces which are not permitting the establishment of new industrial plants until this factory fence provision is brought into effect.
Over the years we have tried-by "we," I mean everybody in Canada who is interested in the preservation of our environment-to get public and private industry to cut back on effluents and make the economy of the country reasonably consistent with the ecology. There are many regulations in the statutes of Canada prohibiting pollution. There are provisions in the Criminal Code against pollution; there are provisions in the Fisheries Act against pollution; there are provisions in the Canada Shipping Act against pollution, and there are provisions in the present water act against pollution. Yet none of these regulations have been properly enforced. If they had, we would not have the serious pollution problem that we are facing today.
Nevertheless, we must face the situation as it is today, and we are now on the verge of passing a water act which we hope will assist in controlling pollution in this country. Without that hope there is no point in considering the legislation. But even though, as the minister has pointed out, this bill has been discussed over the course of many months both in the House and in committee, there are some who still regard its benefits as dubious.
However, regardless of whether the bill will be effective and able to do its job, I want to be sure that it will not make the situation worse rather than better. The proposition that I am advancing is that if the present proposal of the minister as it stands now is accepted, the bill will permit pollution to go on and on, with no time limit within which pollution must be checked. I also suggest that not only will conflicts of jurisdiction arise, but many other difficulties will be encountered unless some time limit is imposed in connection with this effluent discharge fee provision.
This is my reason for moving the amendment. I think it is worthy of acceptance. This principle has been adopted by the minister of fisheries. He has stated that we have to start somewhere, and I agree with him. The minister goes further than I because he says that we have to start cutting back at the factory fence on existing installations. I do not have the opportunity under this bill to go that far, but I do go as far as I can in this amendment,

which provides that this sort of pollution must cease when this bill is passed. The bill must not be used as an excuse for further pollution by new installations.

that Bill C-35, to establish the Canadian Heritage Foundation, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in some ways the very general objectives of this legislation are contained in the title: and act to establish the

Canada Heritage Foundation Act Canadian Heritage Foundation. The purpose of this legislation is to establish a foundation, the primary objective of which would be to encourage the maintenance and preservation of those artistic and architectural treasures of our past which collectively we can describe as the Canadian artistic heritage.
In a few moments I would like to deal with the specific objectives of the foundation as outlined in clause 7 of the proposed legislation, but before I do that I should like to say a few words on the need which this legislation has been designed to meet, for there may be-although I hope there are not-some members in the House who feel that there is no real need for a set of institutions, for government activity or even for private activity, directed toward the preservation of our past. There are those who may argue that Canada is not, like the great states of Europe, the happy possessor of a proud heritage which should be preserved for our future. They might say that our country should look resolutely ahead but not pay too much attention to our roots in the past. Off with the old, on with the new.
I have spoken twice in the House on this general problem; first in November, 1968 and then in 1969. At that time I outlined not only what many other countries are doing but what I felt to be a very great need for increased activity by our government in this area. I do not wish to repeat the arguments that I then made about the importance to the understanding of the country's present, and its future, of the preservation of its past. But I would like to refer, with regard to the general question of need, to remarks made by Sir Kenneth Clark. I do not know how many members of this House have seen that splendid television series which is presented each Thursday night on the CBC called "Civilisation" in which Sir Kenneth Clark describes the history of buildings and their impact on the culture of their times. If you do watch that program, you can see how the spirit and culture of the times is infused in its architecture and its buildings.
At the beginning of the series Sir Kenneth Clark was quoting Ruskin. Ruskin said:
Great nations write their autobiographies in three manuscripts, the book of their deeds, the book of their words and the book of their art. Not one of these books can be understood unless we read the two others, but of the three the only trustworthy one is the last.
Sir Kenneth Clark goes on to say:
On the whole I think this is true. Writers and politicians may come out with all sorts of edifying
May 26, 1970

Canada Heritage Foundation Act sentiments, but they are what is known as declarations of intent. If I had to say which was telling the truth about society, a speech by a Minister of Housing or the actual buildings put up in his time, I should believe the buildings.
I think this general principle is true, that the buildings, the architecture and the art reveal the truth about a society and its time.
In the past, I have spoken about what we should and could be doing in Canada to preserve such historic areas as the port area of Montreal; what should be done to preserve that gracious 18th and 19th century heritage of our buildings. It is a subject about which I feel very strongly because in my constituency every week there are buildings of real historical and architectural interest being destroyed in the name of progress. I have with me, and I will be delighted to show members of the House, a whole publication which has been prepared by King City, Ontario. It was a lovely town, full of early 19th century preconfederation buildings, the attractiveness of which has virtually been destroyed by the disrupting effects of placing a four lane highway running through the middle of it,-a development which the members of the community were powerless to stop.
It may be said by members of the House that the National Historic Sites and Monuments Commission has been designed to deal with this problem and that it is adequate to our needs. For the past two years I have demonstrated in speeches in the House the continuing inadequacies of that commission. What is one to say of a commission which, in over 50 years of existence, has managed to preserve only 30 buildings, or an average of just over one every two years? The type of project which the National Historic Sites and Monuments Commission is directed toward is that of a rather larger project than that of an individual home. They are doing good work at Louisburg, and they have undertaken considerable reconstruction in the Yukon. But they do not have the resources and could not, no matter how generous the government was with funds, have the resources to deal with all of these buildings which are now in private hands and which face, over the next ten years, almost certain destruction unless we take action to help preserve them, to maintain them against the developer's steam shovel and bulldozer.
The problem is an urgent one. We do not have a great deal of time if we wish to preserve this heritage. We cannot do it through direct government activity. We must do it
[Mr. Roberts.!
through encouraging and enabling the citizens of Canada themselves to undertake the restoration and preservation of our architectural heritage. One may ask: do they care? Do they wish to do so? From the correspondence that I have had in relation to this legislation, and from remarks which members of the House have made to me, I am convinced that there is concern. I might just cite one minor example of this, a letter which was written by Mr. Toye of Ottawa which appeared in the Globe and Mail. He was discussing the fact that Batterwood House, the home of the late Right Hon. Vincent Massey, was to be disposed of, including the treasures in that house.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Mr. Toye went on to say:
Just what must one do for Canada to insure that a historical presence will remain after one's departure from the scene? Obviously becoming Canada's first Governor General doesn't do the trick. Philanthropist? Patron of the arts? Forget it!
By the year 2067 maybe, just maybe, someone up in the Funny House on Parliament Hill will hold forth: "Say chaps," he will mutter not too audibly for fear of being heard, "ol' Vincent Massey did just about everything one could do in a lifetime to show us what being a Canadian is all about. Waddya say we buy Batterwood House and all its contents and turn it into a national historical site!"
And it will be done-at ten times the present price to the taxpayer. Assuming, of course, that the treasures sold at auction can be relocated and restored.
And it will be done-assuming that in the meantime the property is not turned into a used car lot. or a Sotheby's Auction House, or a warehouse for Honest Ed.
But, Mr. Speaker, by the time we get to 20o7 that property won't be there, nor its contents. If we wish to preserve the heritage of this country, its architectural and historic heritage, we must do it now, or at least within the next decade, or else we should forget about doing it at all.
Flow do we do it? I have argued in the past that the Historic Sites and Monuments Commission should undertake a much more expanded responsibility in this area, and I have proposed alternatives with respect to the Commission's objectives so that it could do this. However, I must admit that the extent of the problem is so great that we cannot leave it to that Commission alone.
The objective of the Canadian Heritage Foundation that I propose is to provide a means to encourage the citizens of Canada themselves to undertake this necessary task
May 26, 1970	COMMONS
of preservation. Clause 7 of the bill provides the foundation with the power:
-to hold, preserve, maintain, reconstruct, restore and manage the property of the foundation.
If one goes on to subclause (b), one finds, among other things, that the foundation will have power:
-to acquire property, whether by purchase, donation, lease, public subscription, grant, bequest or otherwise.
It will have power:
-to enter into agreement with prospective donors with respect to any conditions governing the use of property.
It can establish trusts in order to do this, and can provide the assistance of experts. It can borrow money, and invest money in order to serve the purposes of the foundation. What kind of things could such a foundation do? How would it work? Why would it help people? Why would it encourage them? What would be the advantage to them, with the assistance of the foundation, of undertaking the necessary work of preservation?
First of all, I would suggest that such a foundation should have a revolving fund, and this fund should have two basic purposes. It would be able to provide interest free loans to householders who had a desire to undertake restoration and improvement of their houses, in order to restore them to their original historic character. I am of course referring to houses constructed before the twentieth century, houses of some architectural or historic interest to the country. This would be a means, at little or no cost to the foundation, of encouraging people to hire the services of restoration architects to preserve the buildings in which they happen to reside and which have an historic interest.
Secondly, and perhaps a more adventurous proposal, although this is a course which is followed to a great extent in the United States, it should be possible for the foundation to purchase a site or building of historic interest, restore it to its original condition, and then resell it with a restrictive covenant to ensure that the historic nature of the building is preserved.
Another important reason for establishing such a foundation is to provide a means by which those who wish to donate or give to the country either works of great art or works of architectural interest may do so and have compensating tax benefits for doing so. At the moment, in order to receive tax free compensation for a gift, the gift must be made to the
DEBATES	7349
Canada Heritage Foundation Act government of Canada or to the provincial governments; in other words, to the Crown. The establishment of such a chartered public foundation would provide a means by which people with buildings or objects of historic interest could transfer them for the use of the people of Canada as a whole and not be penalized for so doing.
Another objective of the foundation would fall in the area of public relations. Many hon. members will be aware of the volume published each month by the American Heritage Publishing Company. Many of us have seen their monthly magazine dealing with historical questions and matters of architectural interest. I am sure such a publication would be too expensive to promote on a profit basis in Canada, but the kind of foundation I have described would be able to undertake such a publication, distribute it to schools, and stimulate a continuing interest on the part of our citizens in the history of our country, and in the architectural buildings which demonstrate the history of our country.
One of the great handicaps in pursuing a steady, consistent and deep program of preservation of our buildings is the present lack in Canada of restoration architects and engineers, equipped and trained to deal with this particular kind of architectural problem. One of the functions of the foundation could be, through scholarships and grants, to provide training facilities and encourage the training of architects and engineers in this area where there is such a great shortage of qualified people.
We have already in Canada many provincial bodies who occupy themselves with the kind of objectives I have described. I do not intend to deal at the moment at any great length with the activities of the Ontario Heritage Foundation, although it is doing much good work. I merely wish to point out that at the national level we need an umbrella, an over-all body which will co-ordinate the very useful work done at the provincial level.
A further objective of the foundation would be for it to work with the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, because the authorities in the United States have found that it is through urban renewal programs that a great deal of very effective work can be done to restore historic areas which have on occasion fallen into the state of slums.
Many people have said to me, "It is all very well to have the kind of program you are describing in cities and countries in Europe, but there is no need for it in North America."
May 26, 1970

Canada Heritage Foundation Act But the United States experience, which is not so far from us, demonstrates the great deal that one can do in the North American scene through government activity. This may be slightly off the subject of the Canadian Heritage Foundation, but to demonstrate the possibilities of action I would like to refer to the Demonstration Cities and Metropolitan Development Act of 1966, passed by the American Congress, which amended another urban development program "to authorize grants specifically to finance historic preservation surveys and planning, for localities of any size." The act gives broad authority for carrying out historic preservation as part of urban renewal.
Agencies carrying out urban renewal projects in the United States now may use project funds to finance surveys to identify historic and architecturally significant property in the renewal areas, and to estimate the costs of its rehabilitation, to acquire and restore such property for resale subject to preservation requirements-I emphasize that this is talking about government activity- and to move historic and architecturally significant buildings to new locations within or outside renewal area. Also, such activities carried out by a locality through local public funds may be credited toward the non-federal share of renewal costs.
In addition, the act authorizes grants to states and local public bodies to help finance public purchase, restoration and improvement of historic and architecturally significant property.
There is a related law in the United States, the Historic Preservation Act of 1966, by which congress created the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, made up of representatives of federal agencies and private individuals appointed by the President. This advisory council has the responsibility to review cases in which a federally assisted or approved undertaking would affect a property listed on the National Register of Historic Sites. Furthermore, federal agencies are required to bring such cases to the advisory council for review before taking final action on any application. If hon. members have time I would be happy to show them some books which indicate the many areas of restoration which have been undertaken by Americans under the authorization of these two acts.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The description of those two acts brings me to the last project which I think the Canadian

Heritage Foundation should undertake, and that is the one of inventories. As a matter of fact, we simply do not know where our historic buildings and buildings of architectural interest are in Canada. We do not have a comprehensive survey of them. On a private basis, in Ontario at least, many groups are trying to do this work in, necessarily, an amateur way rather than a thoroughly professional way, and necessarily without the complete devotion of time that such a task requires. But it is impossible for us to restore, to preserve and respect buildings if we do not know where they are, if we do not know their history and if we do not know their qualities. One of the first functions of the Canadian Heritage Foundation would be to do a national inventory of historic sites, of architecturally interesting sites, those of an aesthetic or cultural appeal which should be preserved.
There is a great deal that such a foundation could do, Mr. Speaker, and a great deal that requires to be done. There is a great deal which the institution of the present Historic Sites and Monuments Commission is not able to do. There are historic considerations, architectural considerations, there are even aesthetic considerations which require us to do much more than we have in the past to preserve our heritage.
The roots of the present are to be found in the past and unless we do something to maintain living examples of the grace, the concerns, the culture of a previous day, it will disappear forever. We cannot do this simply through government action, through government direction and we cannot do it simply through expanded programs of the Historic Sites and Monuments Commission.
We must help the people of Canada to do this for themselves. The problem is too great and the time too short for us to handle it simply through government fiat, government direction, government legislation, but we do have sufficient time if we establish an organization which, through the various means I have described-certain tax advantages, revolving funds which will encourage people to take interestfree loans-can do the things which need to be done. We do have time. We have models which have been used successfully in the United States. There are institutions available which can deal with this problem if we act urgently upon it.
The proposal of the Canadian Heritage Foundation is one which should appeal to members on all sides of this House. It is one which should appeal to a government which
May 26, 1370	COMMONS
is concerned, which is sensitive, to the needs of preserving the evidence of the past in the present. It is a practicable program now, but one which cannot be held up for three or four years or it will no longer be practicable because we will have very little left to preserve. It is one which should recommend itself to all members of this House, and I would urge members on all sides of this House to support it.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to indicate my strong and enthusiastic support for the hon. member, for whose ability I have the highest regard, and for this particular piece of legislation. He mentioned the Canadian heritage and the inferior feeling that some may have who, from time to time, suggest that we are so young that we have little which should concern us in this way. Of course when we compare this land with the ancient civilizations, the Roman, the Greek, the Egyptian, we are very young.
But we have a rich heritage, Mr. Speaker. We have a noble past and we have a hall of heroes and worthy ancestors whom we should honour for the creation of our country. The political process out of which this confederation evolved is not the least among the achievements of nation building in the course of human history.
For too long we have been indifferent to our past, too casual, too careless about our heritage. Too many of those things which symbolize our traditions have disappeared. Many of them have been destroyed and some that were movable have been purchased and have left the country. Indeed, I think we have reached the stage in this country where those things which properly may be designated as historic items and as archival material should not be leaving the country. I am shocked when I read of American universities seeking, and they are likely to succeed, to acquire the manuscripts and papers of some of the great men of letters and men of the political life of our country. I think we have reached the stage where this kind of intellectual and literary nationalism should be exalted.
A situation here in Ottawa recently concerned me greatly and that was the loss of a building rich in history and rich in beauty, both aesthetic and architectonic. I refer to the home of Sir Robert Borden, that beautiful residence called "Glensmere" on Wurtemburg Street. This is the home in which that distinguished Canadian statesman lived for a gen-
DEBATES	7351
Canada Heritage Foundation Act eration, a home to which the great of the world came both in his active life as prime minister and in his many years thereafter as a great elder statesman. Glensmere, which could so easily have become, perhaps, the residence of the Leader of the Opposition or perhaps the locale of the International Development Agency or a shrine whereby we could recall the architect of Canadian independence, fell before the builder's axe. This beautiful home was destroyed and in its place will rise yet another apartment block. Of course, we need apartment blocks and high rise living accommodation, but surely to God, they don't have to be built on the great historic sites of the country.
Perhaps if we had possessed this organization, the Canadian Heritage Foundation, broadly based and sharply oriented, something might have been done before it was too late. Alas, over many many months, the government was insensitive to the need for preserving this historic place. When I presented the idea to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the last session, I received a flippant reply. Months later when I brought it to the attention of the custodian of our culture, the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), I received a gratuitous lecture. As week followed week, the destructive group came closer and now Glensmere is gone and with it a magnificent symbol of one of the great moments of our history when this country moved forward and on to the stage, taking its place on the international scene, moving finally and magnificently from the status of colony to that of full-fledged membership in the world of nations.
Before now in this House I have discussed measures not so precise and not so fully thought out as this one, but I have grieved about our lack of interest in our historic past. I called for more interest in the moments and the places which made for history, of which there are many. These are so often ignored and all the while private individuals are buying up our fine things.
In a few weeks Prince Edward Island will be honouring the Scottish settlement of 1770, a very fine bicentennial and a very important one. This is important. Everywhere we go, we see neglected areas. We see opportunities that have been missed because there has been no leadership and no money. It was our great humorist, Stephen Leacock, who wrote in the "Historical Review" long ago:
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I did not realize that the old grave that stood among the brambles at the foot of our farm was history.
May 26, 1970

Canada Heritage Foundation Act
How many cemeteries alone have been neglected? How poor we are at genealogy; how poor and callous at remembering our great men. Today we have preserved the homes of only two of our prime ministers, out of 15. Every day one reads of some ancient structure being destroyed. In the last few years places in which the Fathers of Confederation lived, men, like Sir Alexander Tilloch Galt, have been destroyed. This we must discontinue. We must not ever become callous and casual in this field. One of the men who adorned this chamber in days past, Arthur Meighen, said:
The story of a nation's heroes is the fountain from which it draws the wine of its later life. There is no inspiration that quickens the ambition of youth, stimulates public service and deepens love of country like the memory of great men who have gone.
I have heard it said that people who ignore their history can be likened to an individual whose memory has gone. One of the tragedies that strikes us is the stage of forgetfulness when only the present touches us. A mature and wise nation honours its past. I think the hon. member who proposed this measure has brought forward a most valuable suggestion. In this I know he is very much in tune with the comment of Joseph Howe. For the fourth time in 13 years I will repeat that statement to this House:
A wise nation preserves its records, gathers up its monuments, decorates the tombs of its illustrious dead, repairs its great public structures, and fosters national pride and love of country, by perpetual reference to the sacrifices and glories of the past.
If Joseph Howe were in this chamber now-he was in this chamber for a while-he would say that the hon. member is doing what should be done, stressing those things that should be stressed and directing our attention to that which ought to occupy our attention. I congratulate him for his effort and endorse heartily his suggestion.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. B. Osier (Winnipeg South Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Roberts) for bringing forward his bill. I think the establishment of a Canadian heritage is long overdue. I like the way the hon. member approaches the subject and the manner in which he stressed its urgency, because the subject is urgent.
We may be doubling our knowledge every four years, or whatever the time is, but surely we are bulldozing under our heritage at least as quickly. No people can be whole if it has no idea of its heritage and no feeling of

continuity with things past. It must be conscious of being part of the ongoing stream and must hand over its heritage to its descendants. We may be a great nation, but our foundations rest upon people of good heart, good brain and good fibre who worked for many hundreds of years to build what we now enjoy. I hope people of future generations will look back on the present generation, on the homes we lived in and the artifacts we used and judge us partly from the environment in which we operated and realize that we helped to bring the country forward.
The hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) spoke very convincingly about the Borden home. He told us what has happened to it as a result of oversight and lack of concern in high places. I think he illustrated the fact that there must be a blend of both public and private concern if we are to preserve some of our history. Men of affairs in high places are too busy to worry about what will happen from day to day in this area. When you approach them they say, "Wait until tomorrow." But tomorrow comes without any action being taken, and on the day after tomorrow the bulldozer moves in-all because our men of affairs are occupied with so many matters that they may forget about our history. People in both the public and private sectors must be concerned in this field and this bill leaves the way open for that concern.
The hon. member for Hillsborough, whom I had not met until coming to this House and who comes from a part of the country far removed from mine, said that in Prince Edward Island they are celebrating the arrival of the first Scottish settlers in the island. On his saying that there was immediately a link between us across the floor of the House and across the country. There is a link between the people he represents and the people I represent. Although we are not celebrating the anniversary of the arrival of Scottish settlers, we in Manitoba are celebrating our 100th birthday and Lord Selkirk, who helped Scottish settlers in Prince Edward Island, also helped and was concerned about Scottish settlers who came to the Red River Valley in the 1800's and who provided the milieu from which a small but adequate civilization grew. That sort of thing links our people be they in Prince Edward Island or elsewhere.
The hon. member for Hillsborough also spoke about Sir Alexander Tilloch Galt, a giant of a man. Most people in Canada do not
May 26, 1970

appreciate that our constitutional discussions, which are of great depth and seriousness, may be repetitions of discussions of earlier days. When you tell them this, they become interested immediately. I know, because I have done that. Some of the great arguments raging today are arguments that raged between Sir Alexander Tilloch Galt and Sir John A. Macdonald. Sir John won the argument, but I am not sure he was right. Perhaps we should look again at Galt's arguments. That would make our constitutional debate much livelier and more interesting for the citizens of Canada. Surely the average citizen of Canada would feel deprived if he knew that because of oversight in high places he cannot obtain a first-hand idea of what Galt's home was like, of the artifacts with which he liked to surround himself, and so on. Luckily we have some idea of how Sir John A. Macdonald lived, because the British government bought his home. We cannot thank ourselves for that.
May I talk once more about our Scottish settlers. There is much greater affinity between the settlers of Manitoba and those of Prince Edward Island than there is between these settlers and those who live just east of us from here. On the shores of Hudson Bay in Manitoba is a place called York Fort, or York Factory, that is subject to a degree of preservation on a sort of ad hoc basis so that it will not completely disappear. This is one of the great and sacred spots in Canada. At the moment it is relatively inaccessible. I say "relatively" because tourists are starting to go there, and oil exploration is being carried out in that part of the country. Overnight the uninhabitable shores of Hudson Bay could become full of shantytowns and boom environment. God help York Fort, or York Factory as it is now called. Surely to God that is sacred ground in Canada. Radisson and Gro-seilliers first landed there. They had the perception to see that the way to get furs was to take a ship in and get the Indians to take the furs down, instead of having to go thousands of miles through extensive river systems.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
The Hudson's Bay Company which owned God knows how much of Canada did all its initial operations through Le Moyne d'Iberville, one of the greatest military minds ever bred in North America to the present day. He was engaged in the only sea battle of any consequence ever fought in Hudson Bay. One day within gunshot sound of Fort Nelson, 22375-47
Canada Heritage Foundation Act which later became York Factory, caught on a lee shoreline three British, Hudson Bay ships came in. He mistook them for his own ships which he had lost in an ice floe some time before. He went out to meet them and discovered that he was outnumbered three to one. He sank one, captured and dismasted the second and sent the third back to England. This was a pretty decisive battle fought by a Canadian in the 1600s. As far as I know there is not a damned thing on that there to commemorate this battle.
Then there is Kelsey who moved west and north. He was probably the first man to see the Prairies. He first realized the significance of the buffalo to the fur trade. It allowed the fur trade to develop food in the form of pemican. It allowed the Hudson's Bay Company and the Northwest Company to move into the north and live and trade in remote spots. It allowed men like Fraser to go to the Arctic. It allowed Mackenzie and other giants of history to open up the country using dried buffalo meat as food.
The port of York Factory lies neglected and rotting. No one has the wisdom to realize that it is important enough to preserve. It will be left until such time as tourists want to get there. This is a big establishment. It was where the first white woman in the west bore a child. She came disguised a boy, chasing her lover who had left her in the Hebrides. She may or may not have caught him. However, she caught something because about 12 months later-
Nine months.

No. That is what is peculiar. Twelve months later she produced a child and went home on the next boat, the following year. Her trip was worth while even though I doubt that she ever caught the lover who left her in the first place.
We also have the Selkirk settlers, Manitoba's version of the Scots who arrived in Prince Edward Island. All these people travelled through this port. Sir George Simpson took over the Hudson's Bay Company when it was almost a complete failure. He took control, rebuilt it and turned it into the most tremendous trading company that the world had known up to that time. He even went to Russia and taught the Russians how to process and market their furs. When Sir George married his cousin and brought her to Fort Garry in Canada to settle, her piano was brought through York Factory, up the Nelson River to Fort Garry.

Canada Heritage Foundation Act
This part of the country in 300 years has seen life, activity, hopes, fears and disappointment. It lies neglected. It is not a little mud fort. It is the very seed place from which my part of the country has grown. It is the seed place of the whole west with its diversity, lust for living and its ethnic groups that give it so much culture and interest in life. It is from here that the facilities they have been able to use were first spawned.
Fort Prince of Wales still lies beside Churchill. It is not in a good state of repair. It is made of stone. It is much more ruggedly built and will probably last a while. Lower Fort Garry, near Winnipeg, has gone except for the gate. It was thrown out a long time ago to make room for real estate development. Fort Gibraltar and Fort Rouge, which predeceased it, were the original forts that went into the founding of Canada. They are gone. There are a handful of houses-probably six, eight or ten-in the whole of Manitoba that are of significant age and significant historical value. Luckily, they have been taken over by people with private means, or interested associations.
There is St. Andrews Church, the first Ecumenical movement in western Canada. The Hudson's Bay Company was determined the settlers would all be Anglicans, and the settlers were all determined that they would be Presbyterians. The Anglican minister preached a Presbyterian sermon and everybody was happy. The Ecumenical movement lasted for 30 or 40 years until the Presbyterians were wealthy enough to send to Kingston to get their own Presbyterian minister. Then all hell broke loose. That church needs to be sandbagged to keep it up. It is a structure of beauty. It is an old, stone church with lovely windows and fixtures. The congregation has moved away. The church stands in a commanding spot on a beautiful curve on the bank of the Red River. In a few years that church will be nothing but rubble unless a few interested people in my part of the world can hook themselves to an organization that has sufficient means to help them preserve that heritage.
What would be the criteria under which this Canadian Heritage Foundation would judge historic sites and their significance? It is bewildering. When I wander around Saint John, New Brunswick, suddenly I feel the United Empire Loyalists come alive. That is no mean feat, because my ancestors were not United Empire Loyalists. Although I have no particular affinity toward them, this is what I feel when I am in Saint John. Port Royal,
[Mr. Osler.l
although a reconstruction, is a good one. I can almost feel Champlain and his merry men there. Fort Henry has been taken over by the provincial government, as a tourist attraction I suppose. It is a good one. But from the point of view of the federal government it could easily have become the ruin toward which it was heading a few years ago.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I have had the pleasure of boating on the Rideau Canal. All one has to do is spend an afternoon reading the historical background on the life of Colonel By, look at some of the stones on the banks of the Canal and at some of the wooden gates to understand the wonderful craftsmanship, engineering skill and workmanship which went into this project. What a crime it would have been had all this been allowed to go. It was nearly let go down the chute; I gather it was only a few years ago that the federal government decided it was worth preserving. Things of this sort are not built today, and they must be preserved.
Go to Batoche on the banks of the Saskatchewan River late in the afternoon and look at the graves of the Metis who were killed in their last, misguided stand against the encroachment of the federal government. Then go into the little church and see the Sunday school notice. The same names are on it as are on the graves, the names of those who died at the battle of Batoche where the dreams of Riel were finally torn asunder.
Not more than two weeks ago I went through MacLeod, Alberta, where there is a reconstruction of old Fort MacLeod. Every Canadian should look at this and ponder over the great feat of the first Mounted Police detachment which headed west and made sure that the whisky traders and the opportunists were held down or stamped out and that the settlers and the Indians who lived there got a relatively square deal.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment that we were discussing at five o'clock was one moved by my colleague from Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken). This amendment was considered for only a few minutes at one of the last
May 26, 1970

Water Resources Programs meetings of the committee, and if you will permit me I should like to read it again; it is very short. It seeks to change the wording of clause 13 (3) in these terms:
"(c) undertake the collection of effluent discharge fees prescribed to be payable by any person for the deposit of waste in those waters"-
The following words are to replace the existing words:
-"but in no case shall an effluent discharge fee be collected for the deposit of waste in respect of any project commenced after the establishment of the agency."
This amendment simply means that no new industry-I suspect it also includes a municipality or any other body-shall allow its waste to contaminate any waters after this act comes into effect. In other words, if a factory is established in a water management area, or for that matter in any area where there is water, it will be required to instal the necessary equipment to prevent pollution of those waters by its waste.
This has been referred to as a factory fence amendment and is something that the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) espoused a while ago. Indeed, he has been talking about it for some time. In the amendments introduced by the minister to the Fisheries Act there is clearly enunciated the principle that an industry will have to instal the necessary equipment or will be required to show proof of such installation before being allowed to discharge its effluent into any body of water.
This has relation to the point we were discussing before. Two of the major bills dealing with pollution-there are others

the Canada Water Act and the Fisheries Act, are quite different one from the other. One provides much stronger measures with respect to effluent that is discharged into waters, which is what this particular amendment deals with. However, one wonders exactly which minister is in charge of pollution control and who is going to win this battle between the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) and the Minister of Fisheries. I suggest that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) should return as soon as possible and straighten out these ministers. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has been arguing that the polluter must pay. I shall in a moment deal with that question in greater detail. He seems to be quite concerned about making headlines and is pretending that he is really going to do something about pollution. On the other hand, the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry seems to be the one who is really
[Mr. Comeau.l
concerned about the matter and is doing something about amending the Fisheries Act.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
This point was referred to when we discussed standards under the previous amendment. Again let me refer to the standards mentioned in the Fisheries Act. In the bill before us the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is not showing a strong hand. So we have these two ministers disagreeing and this amendment brings it to light. They disagree regarding the method by which effluent discharge fees should be applied.

-and it would discriminate against new industries attempting to get established.

-in no case shall an effluent discharge fee be collected for the deposit of waste in respect of any project commenced after the establishment of the agency.
That is to say, after this bill has come into effect. There is an article in today's Globe and Mail with a large headline, "Greene Expects some Pulp Mills to Close Down in Pollution Crackdown." There is a subheading, "Polluter Must Pay." Part of the article reads:
The ethic is always: the polluter must pay. Accordingly, in the event a plant decided to close rather than comply with orders to clean up, the plant would be on its own in weighing the economic pros and cons.
We ask: Why allow an industry to set up in a water basin and then force it to pay an effluent fee under this bill? It is ridiculous. The Minister of Fisheries does not want it. Why cannot this minister agree? We argue that a polluter must pay and that existing municipalities, if they continue polluting, will have to pay. But we say that new industries that are established should not be allowed to pollute. It is very simple for new industries to install the necessary anti-pollution equipment right at the start, rather than wait five or ten years and then be compelled to install it.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources says that existing industries will have to comply and that they will have to
May 26, 1970	COMMONS
install the necessary equipment at this late date. For many years industries have been allowed to pollute. Now the minister says, "I am going to crack down on them. I want them to stop polluting. I am asking them to bring in the necessary equipment to stop pollution." Our position is that new industries should instal the necessary equipment at once. Then no pollution problem would arise in ten years' time.
The purpose of the amendment is to prevent new plants from becoming polluters. The government refused to accept an amendment dealing with pollution standards and now we do not know by how much industries will be allowed to pollute. But we do know that they will be allowed to pollute on payment of a fee. They will not be required to establish the necessary equipment in their plants to stop pollution, as the Minister of Fisheries wants them to do. These are the two points I wanted to make, Mr. Speaker. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will make a speech and let us know exactly what this bill means.

Mr. Speaker, I have been surprised at some of the remarks made by the Parliamentary Secretary with respect to the fear that new plants may wish to locate in areas that are not water management areas. This is back to the old game of designated areas competing against each other. The amendment is an excellent one and the Parliamentary Secretary should consider accepting it. The idea of the factory fence amendment is a good one. I assumed it was original but I find it was advanced previously, and probably was not original even then because with politicians nothing is ever really original.
The Globe and Mail of August 7, 1969, quoted the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) as having said:
Pollution, in other words, must be stopped at the factory fence. It must be confined to our industrial plants themselves. It must not be allowed to spill out into our rivers or to pollute our seas. Instead, it must be limited to the scene of its own beginnings. It must not be allowed to get away. It must not be allowed to contaminate the wholesome environment in which we live.
This is one more minister of the Crown who indicates that a decision has been made that pollution must stop at the factory fence. To me this is a logical development. I have been told that it will cost $200 billion to correct all the pollution of our environment caused by industries and municipalities. It would be doubtful if at election time the government would suggest it had money in that

Will the fee go to the water management agency to enable it to clean up the pollution? If so, it is a pretty useless exercise to have the company provide the money with which to clean up pollution in a new area.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
The Parliamentary Secretary is bright enough to know that eventually we are going to end pollution. We are certainly not going to allow it to continue. I do not think too many people would say that even with $200 billion we could end it overnight, so there would be a time lapse in any case. But we are saying, surely, that inevitably all companies now polluting the waters will have to find a way to cease and desist. The amendment proposed by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) is to the effect that plans will have to be submitted for new plants, no matter whether in a water management area or other area, and that no pollutant will be allowed to destroy the environment. This is logical, in my opinion.
This afternoon I used an example given me by one of my constituents who came from a European company. An article appearing in the Globe and Mail would lead me to believe that the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry has talked to my constituent, because in this article he points out that a similar situation developed in the very rich industrial Ruhr Valley. The minister is quoted as saying:
Take the situation in West Germany, for example. In the Ruhr Valley there are eight million people depending on the flow of a small river-small by Canadian standards-which is also supplying the needs of more than 40 per cent of all of the industry of one of the greatest industrial nations in the world. True, the waters of the Ruhr are being used over and over again. They are being processed and reprocessed. But where the Ruhr enters the Rhine, there is no toxicity. There is no oxygen overload. Fish can live and fish are present in large numbers.
In this article the minister also stated:
One pulp mill, if it is allowed to dump all of its effluent into fresh water, can do as much damage as a city of half a million people. One chemical plant, if it is careless, can destroy an entire fishery. But pulp mills can clean up their "white water". Chemical plants can recycle their wastes, sometimes recovering valuable by-products as well.
It is one of the myths of politics, added to by the politicians and the press, that on the positive side of the Trudeau government is the solidarity of cabinet. I wish there was
May 26, 1970

Water Resources Programs some solidarity of brains in the cabinet. As far as the Minister of Fisheries is concerned, he has solved the problem. Fish can make a very critical assessment of water environment. If the water is not reasonably pure, they die. It is easy for the minister to decide, that before a new chemical plant or a new pulp and paper mill goes into operation it must properly cycle its waste in order to maintain the purity of the environment.
If the cabinet has total solidarity, what gives the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) the right to decide that in waters not under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry industry will have to pay a fine, in effect an effluent fee, to pollute. Why does cabinet allow this minister the luxury of pollution when other ministers say it has to be corrected and will not be extended?
Two government members of the committee were most fearful that there might be competition for industry as between one area and another because areas without water quality management in effect would permit pollution for a fee, whilst those with water quality management would not. Obviously no one in his right mind is going to build a plant in an area with water management control; he is going to build it in an unrestricted area. The whole question of effluent fees revolves around the local management agencies. This fact concerns me because to a large degree the effluent fees will contribute to the administrative costs of the local agencies. These local agencies may not have the necessary expertise. Once particular standards have been established for a basin, the staff and expertise necessary may not be available to take adequate sampling to ensure that their standards, perhaps unsatisfactory, are adhered to.
There has been a lot of discussion in the House this year regarding the problems associated with pesticides, mercuric and other forms of pollution. No mention has been made of thermal pollution, perhaps because of our preoccupation with chemical pollution. The river basins of other countries have had a great many problems with thermal pollution.
I wish to quote from the book "The Frail Ocean" by Wesley Marx. I intend to quote what happened on the Hudson with the Con Edison plant. There was a tremendous problem of fish-kill. This particular passage is by Robert Boyle:
You do not build a power plant on top of a spawning bed of an irreplaceable fish resource. I would no more think of licensing a plant for that area than I would of slaughtering sheep in my living room. It is just not the place.
If the kind of an'i-pollution measures or anti-persuasion measures contemplated in this bill through effluent fees are permitted for existing outfalls as well as new ones, there will be an addition to the total amount of effluent and possible contamination of our river basins. I represent a riding that borders on the Fraser River. My riding is very close to the mouth of the Fraser River. We are very concerned about the estuary of the Fraser River because of its importance in the development of fisheries resources. The problem there is build-up of pollution. Even if there was an agency on the Upper Fraser with certain standards that might be tolerated, there could be a build-up of pollution agents in the bodies of water which flow into the mouth of the Fraser River. A water basin agency on the Lower Fraser would be powerless to control this kind of situation. It would not be in a position to monitor this type of situation. If the introduction of effluent fees is contemplated, it should go hand in hand with the expertise and staff which would make an accurate assessment of the danger being caused.

He said: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis), who is attending to other business relating to this Parliament, I have the pleasure tonight of moving this motion on her behalf. As hon. members know, the hon. lady has been taking a very active interest in the whole question of the impact of phosphorus into the waters of Canada over a considerable period of time. The Hansard record is replete with questions she has raised and references and speeches that she has made on the subject.
Indeed, prior to the introduction of this bill she went so far as to place a bill in her own name on the Order Paper to provide in the Criminal Code that the manufacture and distribution of phosphate in detergents should be made a criminal offence. While this approach as suggested in her bill is not under discussion at the present time, nevertheless the question of banning phosphates is, in effect, the subject matter of the amendment that we now have before us.
As the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway indicated the other evening to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) when she spoke on this bill prior to her departure, this is one aspect of the bill which in general terms we would welcome being added. Indeed, as I listened to the debate this evening, were it not that at this point we are considering the first amendment at the report stage relating to Part III of the bill I would have been very inclined to rise in my place and move the adjournment of the debate. I say that because I think we would be much better off without Parts I and II at all.
I have in mind the fact that some discussion has taken place about the Fisheries Act, the amended version of which was distributed to us just today. I should like the House to give prior consideration to that bill before reaching a conclusion on Parts I and II of this bill. I think following our discussion of that bill, some of the hon. members opposite, including the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Orange), might come to a different point of view. I suspect some of his colleagues might help to do the convincing.
This amendment will put into legislative form a proposal which has been advanced by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources,

namely, the setting of a deadline after which the use of phosphates in the manufacture of detergents will no longer be possible. Hon. members realize that clause 18 of the bill as drafted makes a prohibition but does not spell out any deadline. A few moments ago the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) said that you cannot wave a magic wand and stop pollution overnight. No one in this House will quarrel with that statement. The amendment that we have before us is in effect a recognition of the fact that we cannot say right now that there will be no more phosphate detergents going into the waters anywhere in Canada.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
On the other hand, unless Parliament sees fit to take the necessary action to put a legislative deadline after which it will no longer be legal to manufacture phosphate detergents, I suggest we leave the government wide open to the various kinds of pressures that can develop which might be successful in convincing the government that for this, that or the other reason a further delay in implementing this part of the bill is necessary or desirable for some other reason than that concerned with the improvement of the water quality in Canada.
So I suggest that this amendment in effect will assist the government if the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources means at all that he has been saying in this connection. If he is taking his own statements in this connection more seriously than he obviously has been taking some of his other statements, I suggest we are doing him and the government a favour, to say nothing of the beneficial results to Canadians, in putting forward this amendment and seeking to have it accepted by the House.
The question, of course, becomes quite complicated when one gets into the reason for this concern, which has come about rather suddenly, about the levels of phosphorus in various waters of Canada. The most noteworthy and glaring example of water deterioration is of course to be found in Lake Erie and most of the debate has centered around the situation there. It has been suggested that Lake Erie has become a dead lake. That is not quite correct, as was brought out in the examination of this matter in the Fisheries Committee. Lake Erie, far from being dead is suffering from an overabundance of a certain kind of life. These blooming algae are a form of life. It is their

overmultiplication that has created the situation where the lake and its uses have become less beneficial in many connections including, of course, the commercial fisheries which is one of the major concerns that I have as a member of this House.
So I think that in discussing this amendment and emphasizing the necessity for its incorporation into the bill it is right and proper to bolster the amendment by indicating some of the available evidence on the subject and the reasons why the removal of phosphorus as quickly as possible from Lake Erie and other waters of Canada is a pressing necessity.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources last night spoke at great length about having consulted all the leading scientists on the matter of the maintenance of water quality, without naming a single authority when he was asked to do so. I suggest that had the Minister had a somewhat greater degree of exposure to the information and knowledge that is being disseminated by the Fisheries Research Board of Canada, his speech last night might have taken on a very different tone from that which it did. In saying this I should like to pay tribute to the Fisheries Research Board of Canada and to the work that it has been doing over many years.

The report at page 69 indicates that the most serious water pollution problem in the lower Great Lakes having long-term international significance is the increasing eutrophication of the lakes. It goes on to discuss how this has come about as the result of the luxurious growth of algae and other plants in these waters, and makes it clear that this has happened as a result of the increasing input of fertilizing nutrients from municipal sources, industrial wastes and land drainage.

One of the reasons I have referred to this report is that it makes clear in a balanced way that phosphate detergents are not the only source of the eutrophication that is taking place, but they are the increasing source and they are the source that can be most easily removed. Their argument that we should wait until we have carried out more scientific investigations to see whether or not nitrogen is doing the damage is given the lie by the very text of this report, and they have not advanced any kind of counter-scientific evidence that over balances the weight of the findings of the report.

SPORTS-1976 SUMMER OLYMPICS-IMPLEMENTATION OF WHITE PAPER PROPOSALS TO ASSIST IN PREPARATION OF TEAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, May 28, I put the following question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro):
In view of the fact that Canada has been awarded the Olympic games for 1976, will the minister state whether his department is taking action to implement the proposals in the white paper on amateur sports so that our Canadian teams will be properly prepared?
A few weeks ago the International Olympic Committee paid Canada a great honour by picking this country to be the host country for the 1976 summer Olympics. I must say that great credit goes to the city of Montreal administration, and in particular to Mayor Dra-peau who is one of the greatest salesmen Canada has ever produced. I now come to my greatest concern.
While we may have one of the greatest salesmen, I am concerned that we might not have the best prepared and most competent teams in this field. There is no need for this. Canada is a country with a healthy and competitive young population. We are a sports-loving country and more and more Canadians
DEBATES	7371
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion are taking part in numerous amateur sports. We have many participants in minor leagues and school leagues at the high school and college level. We have old timers' leagues and business and industrial leagues in many sports -softball, hockey, curling, football, touch football, golf, tennis, soccer, rugger, swimming, skiing and so on. But all this participation has not produced people who could play on our national amateur teams. It is true that we have our Nancy Greene, Betsy Clifford, Elaine Tanner, Bev Boys, Bruce Kidd, Harry Jerome, Bill Carruthers and our national equestrian and national bobsled teams, but these have been bright stars in a rather uneven national performance.
The purpose of my intervention at this time is to encourage the minister and the federal government to give every possible support to our national amateur athletic organizations. A few months ago the minister produced a very constructive white paper on amateur sports. There is much in the white paper that could be helpful. I would like to know from the minister or his Parliamentary Secretary if he has authority to implement that white paper, and what progress he has made. I want to encourage our government to help with this program, not just because of the medals we could win but because of the great lift this could give the Canadian people and the basis it would provide for bringing Canadians together in a great national effort, meeting and competing in a friendly way with all nations of the world.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
I remember the great pride we had when Nancy Greene and Anne Heggtveit won their medals. There was a great expression of national enthusiasm. There was even this enthusiasm when our horse Northern Dancer won the Kentucky Derby. I remember people watching their television sets and cheering for Canada, with the hope that this famous horse held out. Let us make sure that we have this enthusiasm often. Let us start with Munich in 1972 and reach a peak in Canada in 1976. We have to start now, Mr. Speaker. The Olympics in 1976 can be a great event for Canada. They could be a much greater event if we produced highly competitive and well prepared teams.

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-RESPONSIBILITY FOR AIRCRAFT SONIC BOOMS OVER LENNOX COUNTY

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. Alkenbrack (Fronlenac-Lennox and Addington):
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-RESPONSIBILITY FOR AIRCRAFT SONIC BOOMS OVER LENNOX COUNTY
speechtext:
I thank Your Honour for giving me the opportunity of raising this matter tonight. On May 7, as recorded at page 6681 of Hansard, I asked the following question:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Minister of National Defence or the Parliamentary Secretary. It results from a long-standing nuisance in the southern part of my riding. There has been a recurrence of sonic booms which in past years resulted in considerable damage in the form of cracked masonry and broken windows for which the government has avoided paying so far.
The actual question reads:
-are Canadian forces planes the cause of the recent frequent and harmful sonic booms which have been taking place over the communities of Bath, Conway and Sandhurst in the southern part of Lennox county?
As Your Honour will note, there was a certain amount of hilarity and levity accom-

panying my question from members on the government side. This is no laughing matter. As early as 1964 I received complaints from houseowners in the village of Bath claiming damage to their footings, foundations, masonry walls, and windows by sonic booms. This was caused by either Canadian or American armed forces' planes practising and training, under NORAD, over Lake Ontario and/or its shores.
Sonic booms can be very harmful, destructive and damaging. The most recent damages were reported on May 6 by houseowners a little further west of Bath along Highway 33. Windows were broken and walls were cracked at Conway, Sandhurst, and in southern parts of South Fredericksburgh township. For those who have never experienced one, let me define a sonic boom. Webster's dictionary defines it as an "explosive sound generated by the accumulation of pressure in a wave preceding an airplane travelling at or above the speed of sound (1,087 feet per second, or 741 miles per hour). Where this wave meets the ground the variation in pressure is experienced as a loud report, and agitation of objects at that point."
In other words, the air is compressed ahead of the airplane and when its trajectory hits the ground it shakes whatever is situated at that point like a dog would shake a rabbit. The tremendous pressure created strikes a house like a battering ram if it is in the line of trajectory. Now, in my complaints of other years to the Minister of National Defence, the incumbent of that time would assume no responsibility because he said planes of the United States Air Force might be responsible and that I would have to provide information as to the date, day, hour and minute on which damage was caused. This information is very difficult to obtain. Even in connection with this last complaint I sought this information but did not receive it.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that regardless of whether Canadian planes or United States planes caused the latest sonic boom damage on the night of Wednesday, May 6, at Sandhurst, NORAD is responsible. This is a joint operation and both nations, the United States and Canada, are jointly and directly responsible for all damage done by these combined forces at any time. Moreover, what a strange and ludicrous anomaly of circumstances we find when Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, a Crown corporation, lends money to citizens to construct houses whose owners must bear the brunt and expense of needless
May 2S, 1970	COMMONS
damage created by another department of government, namely, the Department of National Defence which is destroying those houses. The patient people of Frontenac, Lennox and Addington resent this carelessness and I ask the government to put a stop to it forthwith. I ask the minister to issue instructions to the pilots of our planes and to their United States counterparts in NORAD to carry out their supersonic manoeuvres in some more sparsely populated place.

speechtext:
1. The Superintendent of Insurance is investigating the effect on North West Life Assurance Company of Canada of the reported acquisition of a substantial holding of the shares of NWL Financial Corporation by Residential Resort Developments Limited. The investigation will continue but significant facts are as follows: (a) NWL Financial Corporation is a company incorporated in British Columbia and as a consequence no power exists under federal legislation to restrict the transfer of its shares, (b) Residential Resort Developments Limited is incorporated in the Bahamas and consequently is a nonresident within the definition in the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act. (c) If Residential Resort Developments Limited acquires control of NWL Financial Corporation, the latter will be regarded as a non-resident for purposes of the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act and will be unable to vote the shares that it owns in North West Life Assurance Company of Canada, (d) Residential Resort Developments Limited is recorded as owning enough shares of NWL Financial Corporation to be regarded as a substantial shareholder of North West Life within the meaning of section 33 of the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act. North West Life is therefore prohibited from lending to or investing in the securities of Residential Resort Developments Limited and is also prohibited from lending to or investing in any corporation in which Residential Resort Developments Limited has more than a 10 per cent interest.
