speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (President of the Privy Council) moved
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE AND REVISE
speechtext:
that Bill C-215, respecting the franchise of electors and the election of members to the House of Commons, be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my remarks I thought it might be useful to record the progress which has been made so far this session, and during the present Parliament, with respect to electoral matters. As a starting point I will take the statement which I made to the House on April 1, 1969, which may be found at page 7359 of Hansard for the last session. At that time I proposed the following timetable for dealing with various electoral questions which are before this Parliament. First, I suggested that committee consideration should be given to the report prepared by the Representation Commissioner on the alternative methods of preparing electoral lists, which report was tabled in the House in April of 1968.
Canada Elections Act
Second, I suggested that the general revision of the Canada Elections Act on questions other than election expenses should be undertaken by the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. Third, I proposed the presentation to the House after the committee study of a bill based on that study. Fourth, I suggested that committee consideration be given to the question of election expenses. Fifth, I suggested that the committee review the Representation Commissioner Act as required by section 22 of that statute. Finally, at the suggestion of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) I suggested that consideration, if it be thought generally advisable, be given to the Dominion Controverted Elections Act.
Where, then, do we stand on these various matters? First, the committee studies contemplated in the first two steps in that suggested timetable, namely, the consideration of the Representation Commissioner's report and the general revision of the Canada Elections Act, have now been completed. We are now in the process of engaging in the third step, consideration in the House of a bill based on those changes. With respect to the fifth step, committee review of the Representation Commissioner Act, this matter has already been referred by the House to the committee.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
On the question of election expenses and as a result of discussions which took place at the time of my statement, the House agreed with the suggestion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that that question should be referred to a special committee. I can advise, Mr. Speaker, that a draft motion to make that reference to a special committee has been circulated to representatives of the parties. I would hope to be able to put the motion within a few days and that the House might make the reference before the end of this part of the session so that the committee could be prepared to commence its work by fall at the latest. Assuming successful completion of their work, say by Christmas time, it would then be possible that a bill based on the committee's recommendations with respect to election expenses could be available for enactment before next summer, that is to say, before the summer of 1971.
We are now engaged in study of the bill resulting from the general committee study of the Canada Elections Act. During the time that I have been a member of this House there have been a number of recurrent themes in

May 27, 1970
Canada Elections Act
the criticism of our Elections Act. These themes have included: Why must our election campaigns last so long? Why cannot the system of enumeration be made more effective, particularly with regard to urban dwellers, so that many eligible voters are not left off the voting lists? Why cannot all Canadians abroad be put in a position to exercise their franchise?
In the study of the Elections Act which was carried out by the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections the committee, and subsequently the government, devoted themselves to trying to solve these particular problems so far as they can be solved. The most popular solution which has been put forward, particularly in the editorial pages of the press, has been the establishment of a permanent voters' list. This question, as I have already indicated, was studied by the Representation Commissioner, Mr. Nelson Castonguay, the former Chief Electoral Officer and a person well skilled in these matters, whose report was presented in April, 1968. This report was considered by the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections which committee, in a report tabled in the House on May 22, 1969, concluded that a permanent voters' list would not be appropriate or particularly helpful in dealing with Canadian electoral problems, and the committee reaffirmed that view in the report tabled several months ago.
One can see by reading the Representation Commissioner's report and by perusing his evidence before the Standing Committee that a permanent voters' list is not without disadvantages. What does not appear to be generally known in this country is that in Canada at the federal level we have already tried and rejected a system of permanent voters' lists. In 1934 the Parliament of Canada enacted the Dominion Franchise Act which was to provide a system of permanent voters' lists. The act called for the establishment in 1934 of a basic list of electors, followed by an annual revision between May 15 and July 1. An election was held under this system in October, 1935.
There were 60 days between the date of the issuance of the writ and election day, and a subsequent special committee of the House reported on April 6, 1937, and concluded that the basic lists prepared in 1934 were almost obsolete within six months after they were completed and that the annual revision held in 1935 was not an adequate remedy for the

situation. On the basis of these conclusions Parliament repealed the Dominion Franchise Act in 1938.
In the United Kingdom, despite some favourable comments on the system the permanent list is far from being an ideal solution. We can see this if we examine the timetable involved. The list is reviewed each year and comes into force on February 16 for a period of one year and serves for all elections, national elections and council elections, ordered during that period. Thus, if an election is held in January many people are deprived of their voting rights in the sense that the list has gone stale in the meantime. The same system exists in France, where the list comes into force on the last day of February for one year.
Perhaps the best system of continuous electoral rolls is that existing in Australia where in addition to an annual revision there is compulsory registration and where changes may be made to the list until the day an election is called, which is usually about 30 days before voting day. According to Mr. Castonguay, even though it is mandatory in Australia to register within 21 days following arrival at a new residence, 3 per cent to 5 per cent of the electors ignore this responsibility. Thus, if an election is held six months after the annual revision is completed, the list in Australia really is not up to date, and it probably would be worse in Canada because of the very great mobility of our population.
With our present system, that is to say, a specific enumeration for each campaign, the list is prepared only seven weeks before election day and there is provision for revisions on the nineteenth, eighteenth and seventeenth days before polling day; and in rural polling divisions an elector may vote, even if he is not on the list, by use of the vouching procedure. Apart from the question of the accuracy of a list, it would be very costly to establish a system like the Australian system. Mr. Castonguay, in his evidence before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, stated that-
-to establish the Australian system in Canada, it would easily take a minimum ol $1 per elector per year.
With 13 million electors it would cost at least $13 million a year, as opposed to the expenditure, on an average in every three or four years under our present system, of approximately $7 million to prepare the electoral list. Our system is certainly not perfect but it does offer the advantage that it permits
May 27, 1970

the preparation of lists which are more up to date than those of any of the systems having continuous electoral rolls and at a lesser cost.
My final point on this is a reference to a comment made by a disinterested foreign observer, Mr. Richard Scammon, director of the Election Research Centre at the Government Affairs Institute in Washington, D.C., who appeared last year before the Ontario Committee on Election Laws. He was chairman of the President's Commission on Registration and Voter Participation, established by the late President Kennedy. Mr. Scammon stated before the Ontario select committee: When we were doing our work for President Kennedy five years ago, we had some occasion to look at the Canadian system. Quite frankly, X must confess, I think it is better than ours. I say this, not in the sense of flattery, but simply because the main purpose of any election system, registration of voters, must be to make the task of registration as simple as possible for the non-committed electorate.
If it be accepted that we will not have a permanent voters' list in Canada as recommended by the committee, but retain the system of preparing a special list for each campaign, then we must abandon the hope of shortening the election period by one month. If the essential door-to-door visitation is to take place for the purpose of preparing the voting list, then the whole procedure will essentially have to be retained, including the instruction of enumerators, the period of enumeration over several days so that more than one call may be made on the elector, a period for printing and circulating the voters' list and a further period for correcting errors and omissions in the list by way of revision. The choice is basically between having an election finished in a shorter period of time or having one based on a more up to date voters' list. In Canada we have opted for the second of the two choices and the Standing Committee has confirmed that option.
It is fair to say that even if we did have a permanent list, projections of a shorter campaign, drawn on the English experience, would have to be subjected to scrutiny in Canada. It is obviously easier to run an election campaign in a unitary state which is smaller than at least half a dozen if not more of the constituencies in Canada, and which is very much centralized in communication and transportation. I think it could be expected that in certain parts of Canada, particularly in the case of inclement weather, it could take very much longer to prepare for an elec-22375-50
Canada Elections Act
tion campaign, apart altogether from the question of enumeration even if we did have a permanent voters' list.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
The final word on this question I would give to Mr. Castonguay, who remarked to the committee:
My experience has been that if you talk to an urban member, he feels three weeks are sufficient.
If you talk to a member who has a rural constituency with a large town in it, he will say four or five weeks, but if you talk to a member with a hinterland seat, you will find he would like a lot more than 60 days to cover that constituency.
It is basically for this reason and based on the decision first and foremost that we would not have a permanent voters' list, and secondly because of some of the difficult geography and distances involved in Canadian constituencies, that the government and the committee has felt that the basic pattern of enumeration and the basic election timetable which we have had in our act cannot be changed.
The second of the questions or criticisms to which I refer is why so many people have been left off the voting list. We are familiar with charges in every election campaign that there is a degree of deliberation in leaving voters off the list. Personally, I do not feel that is accurate. The real problem is that in the relatively short time available for enumeration-as I have already noted, some people even feel that time is too long-it is almost impossible for even the most intrepid team of enumerators to make certain, by personal visitation, that every eligible voter in an urban poll is on the electoral list.
I do not hesitate to say that in some cases the reason for an eligible voter being left off the list, in my experience, is his general indifference to the question until it is too late for him to be added under the revision system. I think a great many more are left off, not by indifference or intention but merely because of the basic difficulty in a relatively limited number of visits of contacting people who by pure accident might not be at their residence at the time of the call.
The question is one to which particular attention was given by the government in preparing the bill. I might say one solution which appeals to me personally was our experience under the Elections Act of Ontario whereby urban electors might have a privilege analogous to rural electors of being vouched for at the poll on election day. I have noted, however, that the Ontario committee

May 27. 1970
Ccmada Elections Act
has been casting a critical eye on the practice as it is used in that province and I have found a general feeling among those experienced in elections at the federal level that under some circumstances this system could lead to abuse.
What seems to me, therefore, to be the best compromise under the circumstances is to remain with our present system of enumeration and revision and to seek through more extensive publicity by the Chief Electoral Officer and his appointees, through the public media at the relevant times-that is, at enumeration and during the revision period-to bring to the attention of electors the procedures followed in preparing the voters' lists and the steps that they should take to ensure that their names are on them. I know that the Chief Electoral Officer has been giving some attention to these questions of further and better publicity of the procedure under the act during an election.
The third of the criticisms to which I have referred is one expressed by Canadians who whether in the line of duty or by personal inclination find themselves living abroad at the time of an election. The Elections Act has for many years conferred on all members of the Canadian forces the right to vote in Canadian elections notwithstanding the fact that they are serving abroad. The suggestion has been made that there are many other Canadians living abroad, whether in the line of duty or by inclination, who have not had the right to vote. These would include employees of provincial governments, employees of international agencies such as the United Nations, missionaries, people working voluntarily abroad such as CUSO volunteers, employees of Canadian firms doing business abroad and, perhaps most particularly and most relevant to our immediate experience, members of the federal public service serving abroad including the departments of External Affairs, Industry, Trade and Commerce and Immigration. The conclusion of the committee on this point, which has been concurred in by the government, is that for administrative reasons it should be possible to extend the franchise to members of the federal public service living abroad, but for the same reasons it would be difficult to extend it to the other categories I have mentioned.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, we have a very tight system of control for electors living in Canada requiring, primarily, a personal visitation to determine whether a person is resident in the poll. It is felt that the same 
system of close control should be necessary to avoid a situation where by accident or design someone might appear on a voting list in more than one place. The basic problem with persons living abroad is that of keeping track of them. Through its records the federal government is able to keep track of its own employees-who is living where at a particular time, and particularly at election time- but it is very difficult to keep track of the other categories I have mentioned.
I know this is a controversial question and I take it that it was ultimately decided in committee, as it was by the government, on the basis of administrative difficulty rather than on the basis of principle. The decision of the committee, I take it, was that on the whole there could not be found an effective procedure for assuring that those other than members of the armed forces and Canadian public service employees living abroad would be able to vote without the risk of loss of effective control by the electoral system, and therefore no procedure has been developed to deal with these particular categories.
While I am referring to the special voting rules it might be appropriate to point out one change which was made by the committee and which has been concurred in by the government. It arises out of the requests by Canadian forces electors that the system be changed so that the late reporting of Canadian forces votes, and in the case of the new rules of all the special voters, be overcome and that their votes be counted along with all others on election night. The feeling was that the late reporting of the service vote approximately a week after election night inclined to focus public attention on the party preference of this particular group of electors. This was changed so that the votes of those voting under the special voting rules can be counted with the results on election night. The date for nomination of candidates has been advanced from the 14th to the 21st day preceding voting day, so the forces electors and other special electors may vote from 14 to 9 days before the election.
It will still be possible to segregate a particular category of votes, but under the special rules the preference of a particular category will be less apparent to the community as a whole. It will also overcome the problem known to exist from election to election-the uncertainty of the electoral result in particular constituencies for as long as a week or more. The conclusion of the committee has been that the timetable should be changed in
May 27, 1970

that respect, and the timetable then will affect the dates on which candidates must be nominated in ridings in Canada.
In addition to the foregoing matter, the government has incorporated a great many of the suggestions made by the committee, including the following among the major ones: First, to establish a system of proxy voting whereby fishermen, mariners, prospectors, students and permanently disabled persons may be able to vote at an election through a proxy appointed from among electors in the polling division. It is anticipated that this will add between 5,000 and 6,000 voters to the list or at least give the opportunity to 5,000 or 6,000 people, who otherwise would not have been able to do so to cast a ballot, to exercise their franchise.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The second major change in the size of the electoral group as such is the reduction of the minimum voting age from 21 to 18 years. It has been estimated by the Chief Electoral Officer that this will add approximately one million electors to the electoral rolls. Thirdly, the bill adopts the recommendation of the committee that the right to vote be confined to Canadian citizens and to those British subjects who were qualified at the last general election campaign and who have remained ordinarily resident in Canada on a continuous basis.
Fourthly, it has been determined that for the purpose of determining the place where an elector is to be enumerated, the enumeration date rather than the date of the issue of the election writ should be used. This will mean that a list can be made that is approximately ten days or so more topical than would previously have been possible, thus permitting a much better determination of residence closer to election day.
It has also been determined that a new form of ballot would be introduced-I gather that this is something the committee considered at length-which is intended to overcome some of the confusing aspects of the former ballot form which at times resulted in spoiled ballots. Also, in dealing with the question of spoiled ballots, which were a not insignificant factor in campaigns in the past, I may say that the stricter rules in the existing Elections Act will be relaxed with respect to the marking of ballots so that any mark on the ballot space may be accepted such as, for example, a check mark, a mark with a ballpoint pen or a mark in any other way. They
22375-50^
Canada Elections Act
will be found acceptable and the ballot will not be spoiled so long as the mark is not so distinctive as to identify the elector.
There are a number of points on which the government did not accept in full the recommendation of the Standing Committee. Firstly, while the government accepted the proposal of the committee that the party affiliation of the candidate on behalf of a registered political party should be included on the ballot, the government proposes an increase in the number of candidates at an election for the purpose of determining what group will qualify as a party to be registered. The committee thought that this threshold should be set at 10 per cent of the constituencies, which would mean 26 or 27 nominated candidates under our present system, and that this is a sufficient threshold to determine a party. However, the government has concluded that the threshold should be raised to a higher level for the purpose of determining what constitutes a political party at a national election, that is to say, 75 candidates at an election.
A further aspect which does not appear in the committee's report but which seems to be appropriate under the circumstances is that the qualification for a registered political party under the Elections Act should, alternatively, include any of the political parties which are represented in the Parliament immediately before the election by a minimum number of members, and the figure which has been chosen in the bill for this minimum is the figure which already appears in the Senate and House of Commons Act for the purpose of determining the payment of emoluments to leaders of groups other than the official opposition, that is to say, 12 members. Any party which was represented in the previous Parliament by not less than 12 members will be entitled to be registered as a registered political party, without the necessity of establishing the minimum number of candidates.
The committee was faced, as all of us in the last election campaign were faced, with an anomaly existing between the provisions of the Broadcasting Act which had been adopted one year or so before, and the provisions of the Elections Act concerning broadcasting blackouts. The existing Elections Act provides for a blackout against radio and television broadcasts for two days prior to election day, plus election day itself. The Broadcasting Act reduces the period of blackout to one day, that is to say, to the day

May 27, 1970
Canada Elections Act
before the election day, and to 'election day itself. The committee restored the two-day blackout but the government has not accepted that recommendation and has reduced the blackout to one day prior to the election, and to election day itself.
In addition to these changes, a number of further changes have been proposed by the government in the bill which apparently were not considered in committee. Former section 8, which is succeeded by section 7 in the new bill, declared vacant the position of returning officers in each of the electoral districts across Canada. This was a practice followed when the Elections Act was last generally amended and re-enacted in 1980. But the Chief Electoral Officer points out that this involves a considerable dislocation in the election administration, and that it would complicate his already not inconsiderable administrative problems or tasks involved in preparing for an election under the new system if all the positions of returning officers were to be declared vacant. On this basis the new act departs from the practice followed in the 1960 bin.
Another matter which I gather was considered in the committee and rejected was the suggestion that not only should the minimum age of a voter be set at 18 years but that the age of eligibility for being a candidate should be at the same level. The government has concluded that if 18-year old citizens are to have the right of casting a vote at an election, they should equally have the right to stand for election after the usual nomination procedures have been followed. On that basis, the qualifications of a candidate have been stated as anyone qualified as a elector, which of course includes those who are 18 years old or more.
One question which I believe occupied much of the time of the committee was the effect of provincial laws, if the change were implemented, on the possible legal liabilities of an 18-year old candidate, particularly in the matter of contracting for supplies and services in an election campaign. The question was debated at length, I gather, as to whether it was desirable or even constitutional to include a provision in the Elections Act reducing the age of legal majority for these purposes to 18 years even though in some provinces-Ontario, for example-the age of legal majority remains at 21 years.
In view of the possibility that in the near future many provinces may change their law on this question of the legal age of majority,

and also because certain of the provinces already have changed the law and there is variation in treatment with regard to this matter, the government concluded that it was best to leave it to the law of any particular province to determine the matter of liability of the candidate. The only warning and free legal opinion I would offer to any contractor in Ontario undertaking to supply an 18-year old candidate is this: He should make certain that he receives an undertaking from a person of legal age for the payment of all debts. However, as was said at a public meeting which I attended last week, a fair number of 21-year old and older candidates who have become bad debt risks.

The Chairman of the committee might have a few comments to make on this subject. I believe the committee discussed the matter with provincial commissions and committees of the provincial legislative assemblies. However, I do not believe

perhaps I should consult my colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner)-that any specific bill to reduce the legal age throughout Canada is contemplated.

speechtext:
I say to Your Honour, the minister and my colleagues that I welcome the legislation which is now being debated at second reading stage. We have waited a long time for it. Some of us in this House have been asking for a good many years to have the Canada Elections Act reviewed and studied by a committee. It has been a long-standing practice that following every federal election the document is referred to the appropriate Standing Committee for suggested amendments and improvements. While we have waited a long time, we are pleased that at long last it is before this House.
This is a very important matter, Mr. Speaker, dealing as it does with the mechanics of a democratic government. What laws we in this chamber pass are, of course, important, but how we get here and how our public institutions are constituted and structured is, I submit, a matter of even greater import. I am confident that, as is usually the case in matters of this kind, the members of the House will approach this legislation with a minimum of partisanship and a maximum of desire to do what we can to improve the electoral machinery of this country.
The question of who has the right to vote and how the vote is taken is a matter of vital significance in any political democracy. We in this country have legislation which is honest, efficient and can properly be called a worthy vehicle of political democracy. We are fortunate in having a most excellent man at the head of operations in our electoral process. The impartiality, competence and dedication of the Chief Electoral Officer, Mr. Hamel, commands the respect and confidence of all members of this House.

Canada Elections Act

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE AND REVISE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
The purity of our election machinery and the probity of our election officials was not always an earmark of our Canadian society. The idea of one man, one vote, secrecy of the vote, ease and freedom of the voting process was by no means the case in this country nor in many other countries which call themselves democracies, parliamentary or otherwise, a couple of centuries ago.
Thomas Paine, that great tribune of freedom, wrote as "men are born, and always continue, free and equal" and as "the end of all political associations is the preservation of the nature and imprescriptible rights of man"-it followed "the right of voting for representatives is the primary right by which other rights are protected. To take away this right is to reduce man to slavery, for slavery consists in being subject to the will of another, and he that has not a vote in the election of representatives is in this class. The proposal, therefore, to disfranchise any class of men is as criminal as the proposal to take away property."
For a long time members of the community were denied the right to vote. Until the government of Sir Robert Borden and later the government of Arthur Meighen, women-that delightful section of our society-were not entrusted with the right to cast ballots. I suppose there is no one in the chamber old enough to remember when that happened. But it is not too long ago. To the historian it is merely yesterday. For a long time, too long, those who did not own real estate were shut out from the electoral process. Some of those who did own real estate were frequently given multiple votes. The man with much of this world's goods would have several votes, and the man less endowed would have no vote.
In some parts of the world devices were found to deny the franchise to certain groups in society for religious, ethnic or racial rea-s,ons. I am not just thinking of the deep south of the United States in recent years, South Africa, Rhodesia or parts of Europe; I am thinking of something a good deal closer to home. Under the administration of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) the Indian people of this country were given their full and proper place in this electorate. This is a matter of only a few years ago.
IMr. MacquarrieJ
Today through this legislation we are extending further the franchise by the extension of the right to vote to those who in some legal sense are regarded as infants, namely, those between the ages of 18 and 21, or more properly put, under the age of 21. While I welcome this development because I always like to get the whole story on the record, I cannot refrain from saying that this government and this Parliament have been dragging their feet on the question. Many countries in the world long ago extended the franchise to those under the age of 21 years. An interesting example is the state of Israel. At the very inception of the establishment of that country the voting age was fixed at 18. In this country many of the provinces have shown leadership which the federal government is now following. I salute the provinces which made the advance in this field. Prince Edward Island, Quebec, Manitoba and Saskatchewan have set the voting age at 18. British Columbia, Alberta and Newfoundland, for reasons I cannot understand, have set 19 as the magic age. Now the Dominion is moving in that direction.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
During the last 13 years many members of this House have presented private members' bills urging just such a course of action. While deploring the previous insensitivity of the government, I wholeheartedly give this measure my support and congratulate them on their belated conversion to this idea. In saying this, I do not withdraw the criticism I made earlier this session concerning the presumptuous arrogance of the government in forecasting this legislation in the Speech from the Throne, thereby showing contempt for a committee which had been charged with responsibility for examining the whole question of the voting age.
I have long believed that 21 was an unrealistic age to have chosen. The retention of this age is an interesting example of the retention of the archaic in modern times. A couple of years ago the United Kingdom Parliament set up a parliamentary committee on the age of majority. This committee produced one of the most interesting and readable documents I have ever had the opportunity of perusing. At page 20 of the report of the committee-Command Paper No. 3342 issued by Her Majesty's Stationery Office in 1967-we read under the heading "Historical Background-How the Age of 21 Evolved":
The fact that the later law of infancy has been constructed from the piecing together of a mass of
May 27, 1970

exceptions to an archaic principle has rendered it difficult and obscure. We who write history ought not to complain of survival; but in this instance we must admit the deplorable effect of this particular survival.
The quotation is from Holdsworth's "History of English Law". The report goes on to say:
In Roman law young people were divided, like Gaul, into three parts. First, there was infantia which was ultimately fixed as under 7-it is perhaps ironical that it is this word whose descendant has come to be used in our law for everyone under 21-
Roman historians state that the barbarians reckoned their young were old enough to carry arms and be counted as grown up at 15. And 15 became the general age of majority in Britain and northern Europe during the ninth, tenth and eleventh centuries, though not specifically linked with fighting ability. But by the time of the Norman Conquest there was a change of emphasis. The role of the mounted knight became more and more important, the armour heavier and heavier and the horses more enormous as time went on. By the time of Magna Carta the age for those holding in knight service had been raised to 21 and there is strong authority for the view that this was directly linked with the ability to hold up a heavy suit of armour and lift a lance or sword at the same time.
It was said, for example, that the profession of arms demanded an ability and strength not to be acquired until the age of 21. I mention these things in case there might be some who believe there is something sacrosanct about the age of 21.
It was interesting to hear the exchange between the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) and the minister. I think the minister was wise in being something less than precise in his replies. I can foresee a curious situation in which people would move in and out of infantile status as they moved from province to province. I think the minister was wise in withholding a full and considered reply on that aspect.
The British, it seems to me, showed their usual wisdom in parliamentary matters when rather than looking only at the question of the voting age they examined in detail the whole subject of majority. I might say that the committee to which I have alluded did in the end recommend that the age of majority be set at age 18. Of course, here in Canada we have multiple jurisdictions, the sine qua non of federalism, and the process will take more time. Still, it is something to which we should and must come because in terms of educational attainment, to mention only one field, there is no question but that present-day students are the recipients of a far more inten-
Canada Elections Act
sive and advanced course of training than were even those of us who are so young as to be merely at the half century mark.
While parents and educators-and I belong to both groups-are perhaps reluctant to admit the superiority of some things in the contemporary scene, I am confident as I look at what is going on in our schools that our young people are being presented with a far heavier and more varied curriculum than was available to us in our day. In many senses, people of 18 are at the apex of their physical and intellectual strength, or perhaps I should say capacity. I do not use the phrase moral or spiritual maturity because that is something which comes much later-a quality indeed which may not come at all to some people. On the other hand, there is likely to be a high degree of idealism and a lesser degree of absorption in the tedium of day-to-day routine. Perhaps it is in these years that a sensitive person comes closest to John Keats' ideal of a civilized person as being one to whom the miseries of this world are misery. It is a time of disinterested interest, if I may use a seemingly paradoxical expression.
I notice there are some sectors of this group between the ages of 18 and 21 which have shown no great enthusiasm for the franchise. This surprises me a bit and pains me a little. I am enthusiastic about the move. I have been enthusiastic for a great many years, not because I think it is so popular among the group about to be 'enfranchised but because of what it can and should do for the political process in enabling political parties in a democracy to flourish. Lord Bryce explained this long ago when he pointed out that political parties are older than democracy and that no great free state can function without them. As he said, no one has shown how representative democracy can work without them. In the political process and in the party structure surely everyone would concede that we can derive much from the ebullience, the idealism and occasionally the irreverence of youth. Where do we see the young, whether they be long-haired or short-haired, today? We see them in the streets demonstrating, protesting, parading. Sometimes we may be tempted to think that they are wrong, misguided or perhaps covertly directed by somebody or by some group which really does not have much idealism but something more mundane or sinister in mind.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
However, I believe that whatever the situation, whatever the auspices and whoever the

May 27, 1970
Canada Elections Act
stimulators, there is an energy, drive, commitment, dedication and concern among youth. I believe that a healthy, vital political party should not be content if these people are on the streets and not in the council rooms of the party. I am convinced that this is where the value may come in. I think the fulsome participation of those who are now too young to vote in political parties and in the democratic process generally will and should enliven our political institutions, make them more relevant, perhaps even more exciting. This new section of the electorate will, I am confident, add some elan, some action and some willingness to tread paths that some have said should not be trodden and others have said could not be trodden successfully.
There are some interesting items in the bill which were not reflected or recommended by the committee. I note the distinction between 18 and 21 in the age of candidates. It would seem to me that with candidates seeking to represent an electorate that is age 18 and over, there should not be any hiatus signifying that the candidates must be in that portion of the electorate which falls not within the years 18 to 21. In this instance I would say-and perhaps this is the last time I will say it-the government has improved on the recommendations of the committee. I thought it was inconsistent that the electorate should be 18 and that the people who represent them were required to be 21.
But there still remains the interesting anomaly which perhaps only lawyers can find needed satisfaction from, that while the voters need be only 18 and the candidate need be only 18, the returning officer must be 21. I think that returning officers are very important people in elections, but I do not think they are any more important than the electors or the people upon whom the electors pass judgment on election day. I think that is one little anomaly that is not, in my judgment, impressive. I do not think it is any more onerous a job than being a candidate or being a Member of Parliament. I do not think that the responsibility of a returning officer is all that great that he has to have these extra three years before he takes on his particular chore on election day.
There are some other items I should mention. Although I have been churning away, agitating for this measure to come before the House for many years now, I assure my colleagues that I have not been saving up all my thoughts and potential speeches, and that I

have no intention of unburdening myself at length today. The question of political affiliation is one which troubled me, and in this field I must confess to a conversion. When I had the honour of chairing this committee in the twenty-fourth Parliament I was stoutly opposed to the addition of the party label to the ballot. Being a good chairman, of course, like the present chairman, I would not have thought for one moment of inflicting my views on the committee, but I did think that that was a mistake. I thought it denigrated and downgraded the role of the candidate and overexalted the situation with respect to the party. I had in my mind the extreme case of the list system used in the Weimar Republic of Germany, where the proportional voting system and the list system brought about a situation whereby at a certain stage people were automatically sent into the Reichstag because their particular party had received a certain proportion of the votes. The individuality of the representative was a non-factor in the whole affair.
I am impressed by the increase from 26 to 75 candidates. This was not what you might call a burst of generosity on the part of the government. I did not think that the minister was too lucid or helpful in explaining why the 26 to 75 bump was insisted upon by the government. Perhaps when we reach the appropriate section of the bill at a later stage the minister will elucidate and tell the House the virtues and values of this particular change. There is always a problem, of course, when you get into the situation of the state taking formal note of political parties. For many years our political structure in a formal way knew not political parties. They were things that existed alongside the constitutional structure. But when you have the state recognizing this party and that party, you are into an area where the state and those charged with responsibility in this matter must tread carefully. However, in the long run I think it is perhaps helpful to have the party affiliation on the ballot. I do not know why it is important that the occupation be taken off, but I do think it helpful to have the political affiliation put on. I think we can count on the wisdom and good judgment of the Chief Electoral Officer to assure the proper working of the relevant parts of the act, which I expect will pass.
Although the minister did not mention it, I think a slight change has been made in connection with citizenship and British subjects.
I believe the governmental recommendation is
May 27, 1970

a little more restrictive than was that of the committee. Again, I do not know why this change has been made. There are two aspects to this question, of course. If you look at the question from the view-point of non-discrimination between various groups of people who have come to Canada from other countries, you may have one point of view. If you look at the question on the basis of the reciprocal franchise arrangement between the United Kingdom and Canada, then you might reflect upon the matter in a different way. On June 18 there will be Canadian citizens fully entitled to vote in the United Kingdom election. So that if this measure does go through, no longer will there be reciprocation from us in regard to extending the franchise to Canadian citizens who are properly domiciled in the United Kingdom at the time of the enumeration of the permanent list.
The proxy vote is an improvement. It will, as the minister says, allow people to vote who under the existing legislation would have neither the opportunity nor the mechanism to vote. However, it should be remembered that a proxy vote is a diluted or potentially diluted vote. It is something a little less than the voter himself actually marking his own ballot. It is not a substitute for his vote and it not a substitute for the absentee voting system which prevails in many countries.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I listened carefully to the minister when he spoke about the whole issue of the establishment of the permanent roll. He quoted from the Representation Commissioner's report. I have read the Representation Commissioner's report. I have heard his views many times and have the greatest respect for him. But on this matter, despite his strong arguments against the permanent voters' list I am very much like the old Presbyterian elder about whom John Buchan writes. The minister was castigating the old fellow for his views. He said to him that St. Paul had said thus, and so whereupon the elder said, "On this matter St. Paul and I disagree". I still think we will never have a satisfactory and really efficient voting system here until we do adopt the permanent list. It is all very well to say that the United Kingdom is a unitary state and a small country, smaller than parts of Canada, but I point out that the United Kingdom elects 630 members, quite a few more than we do, and they have an election in a month. They seem to do it very well.
Canada Elections Act
I would point out, also, that while it is very costly to establish a permanent list, anyone who has any idea that Canadian elections are cheap is not reading carefully the financial statistics of this country. It costs a great deal to rim an election in Canada. I do not have to rest my case on the economics nor on the quotations to which the minister referred. One of the most populous countries of the world, India, is a federal state. Everyone knows India must have some of the same problems in respect of distance that we have, and other problems which we do not have in this country. However, India, with all its difficulties, is establishing a permanent voting list.
I think with a permanent voting list one would not require the proxy vote. One could have a temporary residence in many parts of the world and have an absentee ballot. This could overcome a great many problems. I am delighted to note that federal civil servants and their dependants abroad will be given an opportunity to cast their vote. But I do not like to see private citizens abroad denied that opportunity. If we had a proper, fully established voting list we could, through the vehicle of the absentee vote, allow for this sort of thing. We all know that many United States citizens who are domiciled here can, through the absentee ballot, participate in the elections in their particular state. The minister says that if a list is drawn up at a given time of the year some people will be lost when the election comes up. Did we ever have an election in Canada when we did not lose a number of people? There are always people who are, unfortunately, not able to vote.
In one famous election which the federal government called quickly and hopefully, thousands of students were unable to cast their ballots. Our system is not perfect and under this legislation we will lose all sorts of people who will be abroad. We live in a mobile society. More and more people will not be sitting in their constituencies waiting for someone to call an election. I do not think we have yet faced up realistically to the question of the permanent list. I still hold to the view that this is the answer to which we should address ourselves.
I am interested in and pleased with the new ballot design. We are to have a little style on the back of the ballot and a circle on the right-hand side following the name. This will be interesting. I am also pleased that we have broken away from the restriction that the ballot must be marked with an "X" by a

May 27, 1970
Canada Elections Act
pencil provided. We all know that in the age of the ballpoint pen people very easily mark an "X" with that.

speechtext:
Yes, some of the pencils are taken. I would never take one with a string attached to it, but if the string were not there the pencil might pop into my pocket inadvertently. Here I should like to pay tribute to the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Code) who carried the torch in respect of this particular amendment. He has had personal experience of ballots being well and truly marked with something other than the pencil provided. I believe we should call this particular amendment the Code amendment because he is the author of it. I believe it is an improvement. We know the reason the provision was there: it was to preclude, prevent or diminish the possibility of identification. But during all the years of the Canadian forces regulations we had no problem although members of the forces were allowed to write the whole name in red, green, yellow or what have you. So I believe this amendment is an improvement.
I think the form of the ballot is interesting. Here, to show our ecumenical inspiration, I believe we are following the ballot that has been developed and used in Belgium. I believe the merging of the service votes is a help. Many members previously had to wait for the service vote to come in, and if they did not belong to the Liberal Party they probably waited in suspense for their defeat. Now, by moving the official nomination a week ahead and thereby linking the time for taking the military vote we have this vote coming out on the same day. This will make the situation similar to that of the advance poll. This is an improvement and I think we will all agree with it. Perhaps it would be even better if the military service vote was not only merged in time but merged in the general stream of the electorate. This, however, is not in the act at the present time.
I did not hear any convincing argument in the minister's statement on the question of the blackout on broadcasting being reduced from 48 to 24 hours. He said the committee restored the 48 hours. I say to him with respect, that is not the situation. It was not restored by the committee. The Canada Elections Act had never moved away from the 48-hour blackout. Since it was the Broadcasting Act which cited 24 hours in the case of the holding of elections, naturally the Canada 
Elections Act prevailed. I should like to hear the reason this is now considered to be an improvement. I do not think it is a bad thing to have a closing-out of the appeal through the media over Saturday and Sunday. Heaven knows, it is not a bad thing for the candidate and I have a feeling it is not a bad thing for the long-suffering electorate which has been subjected to appeal after appeal for many weeks beforehand. So I wonder why the government in its wisdom made that change.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
One thing I liked, too-we talked about this a good deal in the committee-is what I call the civilianization of the Canadian forces vote. I never liked the idea that one had to go to some military base, seek out the commanding officer and examine there the list to see if there were people on it who were electors in a given constituency. Now that these lists will be despatched by the Chief Electoral Officer to the returning officer in each constituency and then made available to the candidates, the situation will be much improved. I am heartily in favour of it.
I thought that the minister might have been a little more generous to the committee. It struck me that in the recent publicity and in the minister's speech today there was a feeling that the government was bringing its child to the baptismal font. That is the case technically with a piece of legislation that must emanate from the government, but I would like to submit that the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Laflamme), the chairman of the committee, is far more the father of these improvements and amendments than is the minister or this government.

I thought that the minister might have found a minute or two to pay tribute to a very hardworking man. Although we had a little "set-to" at the beginning, I would say he was a very fair man and a very good chairman, and I salute his dedication to his work. I found it a great pleasure to work with him. I also want to commend the members of the committee. I had both the honour and the onerous duty of presiding over the committee when the 1960 amended act emerged. It is a very time-consuming, difficult, challenging and important task and I have the highest regard for the members of the committee who served and who came up with excellent ideas. It struck me that in the
May 27, 1970

discussions in the committee, partisanship was always left outside the door and we all worked as well as we could to improve our machinery for the electoral process. I am particularly grateful to colleagues in my party who functioned on the committee while I happened to be away in the Middle East for two or three weeks where there were other problems to deal with. I think my colleagues did a wonderful job.
I am not going to speak on the item of the relaxation of the liquor laws. Under this new dispensation, so far as this act is concerned, the booze shops need not stay closed for the whole day and after the election is over they can open the doors so far as this act is concerned. For different reasons there is sometimes a desire to seek consolation or extra jubilation on the evening of election day, and this may not be a bad idea. I am not making a personal plea in this case but rather a general observation. I noted in particular the minister's reference to the continuity of election officers even though a new act may emerge from time to time. This protection of officialdom is interesting and we will watch with considerable interest whether this protective instinct is extended to other areas of the national administration.
I welcome this piece of legislation and I will support it. We will have some amendments, we will have an interesting discussion, but it is my prediction and view that there will be no protracted delay in this important matter. I do regret that it was necessary to change some of the recommendations of the committee which did a good job. I do not want to make comparisons, but I remember that the committee report of 1960 was adopted by the government of that day without the kind of alterations which this present government found necessary, and oddly enough in 1960 the expression "participatory democracy" was not used very much.
In conclusion I should like to say that I give my support and I welcome this progressive move. I hope we will not end here but will continue to look at the question of the permanent voters' list and other means whereby we can make a good piece of election machinery even better.
