Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that an item such as the electoral law is considered by too many people to be somewhat a dull subject. It might be the view of many members of this 'House that it does not have much political sex to it which might enliven the debate or stir up massive public interest, let alone stir up interest among members of this House. In order to do so the minister might, in leading off, have tried to put some political sex into the bill and into his speech to encourage the rest of us to do the same thing, and he could have entitled his speech "Rolling in the Grass-Roots".
I add my congratulations to those of the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) to the members of the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. I admit that both my hon. friend and myself are somewhat prejudiced since we were members of that committee, but we spent scores of hours and

candidate for office, to form a party and run candidates or otherwise participate in the electoral process. Nor must the law discriminate in favour of a governing party or one or more established parties so as to impede unjustly the electorate from replacing those who govern them. Third, to as great a degree as possible the law should be simplicity in itself, so as to be most easily readable and understandable, to be easily abided by yet readily enforceable if broken.
Fourth, throughout all its provisions the law should have, in this order, regard for the voters, regard for the parties and the individuals representing them who are seeking elected office, and lastly regard as to administration and the efficiency of its operation. Fifth, the law should contain safeguards that serve to enhance the rights of electors and of those seeking election, as well as to prevent abuse. I would like to emphasize this point. This should be the first priority in the safeguards, that they enhance the rights of electors and of those seeking election, as well as to prevent abuse. Further, the law should contain penalties, which can be easily enforced, to deal with any elector, candidate, party or corporation that corrupts the law and perverts the democratic electoral process. Sixth, in the context of convenience, firstly for electors and those seeking to be elected, the law should be as administratively simple and efficient as possible, but administrative difficulty and greater cost should be accepted rather than lessening any opportunity for electors to participate.
I have tried to outline some fundamental principles that I think our election law should embody. No doubt other hon. members could state them better than I, add to them or expend on them, and I invite them to do so during this second reading debate. Now, turning to Bill C-215 may X try to examine how well some of its provisions meet these basic principles necessary in an electoral law for a democratic party system peculiar to Canada. How does the bill measure up to these principles? In increasing the eligibility of and maximizing the opportunities for citizens to vote, the bill has a number of improvements yet still falls short in several ways of fulfilling the first principle I outlined. Lowering the age eligibility of electors, candidates and election officials to 18 is a long-overdue improvement. It is about 25 years late, Mr. Speaker. I say that with some pride because my party and my province were the first to implement this principle nearly 26 years ago.
Canada Elections Act
I am perfectly happy that the government and the minister chose not to agree with a majority committee recommendation concerning the age of candidates. That was one of the few occasions in the committee when discussion became warm, if not heated, namely, when a majority of the committee felt that the eligible age of candidates should be kept at 21. I am glad the government and the minister disagreed with that recommendation and have in fact made provision in the bill for candidates to be age 18. I see no legal problem here, based on the experience in my own province of Saskatchewan. It is a rare case when any political party nominates anyone under 21, but it always has the right and the opportunity to do so if it wishes, and those under 21 have the right to stand for nomination. Even were it to happen, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the likelihood of any difficulty as between the age of the candidate and the legal age is so remote that we should in no way impinge upon the right to be a candidate at age 18.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The clause establishing residence as of enumeration day instead of the day of the election writ is a minor but good change. Improvements in enumeration and revising procedures should at least slightly increase the number of eligible voters. Proxy voting increases the opportunity for more people to vote, but because of the dangers inherent in such a system the provisions in the bill are necessarily restricted and narrow and still leave out a large number of people. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that experience will prove it to be a system that is cumbersome to administer and, at best, inconvenient to use.
There is one thing that I think goes against the grain of any citizen, and that is the possibility of one person casting a ballot for another. The provisions of the proxy system in this bill, particularly for those who are crippled or bed-ridden, is a marvellous move and will no doubt be of benefit as well to prospectors, mariners, fishermen and students. However, it still leaves out large numbers of people who because of their occupation will be absent from their usual place of residence as long as, or perhaps even longer than the people provided for in the bill. This points up what I submit is a major deficiency in the bill, the lack of an absentee ballot system no matter how circumscribed it may be.
In the 1968 general election 2,642,972 Canadians did not vote, that is 24 per cent of
740G

May 27, 1970
Canada Elections Act
the electors on the voters' list. Even though the percentage of turnout was good compared with other elections in Canada and compared with other countries, it still means that far too many people did not exercise their franchise. No doubt some chose not to. But how many of them were prevented from voting by the inadequacies and restrictions contained in our Elections Act? How many tens of thousands more who were not enumerated, who did not and could not vote, could be added to this figure? We will never know how many. But there is no question that a large number of electors were eliminated from the electoral process because of the inadequate provision for advance polling and because of no provision for absentee balloting.
In a country as large as Canada and with a population as thinly scattered as ours, I fully appreciate the great administrative difficulties that a system of absentee balloting presents. I base this statement on personal experience. I fully appreciate the administrative difficulties pointed out when the subject was discussed in committee. But surely, Mr. Speaker, administrative problems should not be allowed to prevent the widening of opportunity for people to vote. There are many variations of an absentee ballot system that can be used. Surely we are capable of adopting ways of overcoming or at least minimizing administrative problems.
I am not satisfied that the committee, the government or this House have given sufficient attention to this question. There has been too great a readiness to discuss reasons why absentee balloting cannot be carried out and then to discard the idea. Not nearly enough attention has been given to arriving at how it can be done. The debate on this bill gives us our last chance to do something about the matter. Let's get at it. Our election law receives substantial revision at best every 8, 10 or 12 years. Surely we must make a further effort now in as bipartisan, positive and objective manner as we can to come up with a method of absentee balloting for the tens of thousands who will be prevented from casting a ballot.
The advance poll provisions are still the same, and I submit they are inadequate. A further method of enlarging the opportunity for electors to vote is to increase the number of days for advance polling. The addition of federal public servants and their dependants to the electoral rolls with the armed forces overseas is a step which we approve, even

though some might still consider there is a problem concerning identification of their vote because the results are published separately. However, the provision to announce the results of votes cast under the special voting rules by each returning officer no earlier than one hour after the polls close on election night seems to further diffuse the problem of identification and distract specific attention from those results. I suggest that a further way to lessen this problem would be for the returning officers to lump the armed forces and overseas vote results with the total advance poll results and announce them in one aggregate total on election night. It would mean that the ballots cast by those in our armed forces and those overseas would get even less specific attention. I hope the minister will think about that suggestion between now and the committee stage and agree that it would be an improvement.
There are still too many people who should be able to vote and cannot because they are not provided for, or are in this bill prohibited from being electors. The minister has mentioned this matter. What about CUSO volunteers, students and tourists who are temporarily overseas at the time of an election, or civilian employees of private business permanently stationed outside Canada? These groups will total in the thousands though the number will fluctuate widely from time to time. I submit that here is an important avenue for some sort of modified absentee balloting system.
Why could not these people, before leaving the country appear before the returning officer in their constituency and attain a certificate proving residence and eligibility to qualify as an elector in the constituency? Then, when a citizen is overseas this document could be presented to the nearest Canadian embassy, consulate or designated office at the time of a general election and he could be allowed to cast an absentee ballot. It could then be mailed to the Chief Electoral Officer and be counted, and the result passed to the appropriate returning officer. I throw this suggestion out as one of many ideas that have been discussed and examined. It is not original, but it seems to me it is a modified version of absentee balloting that could be applied when people are overseas. Surely we can devise such a system and include it in the special voting rules. What about the thousands of people in Canada who are working in the construction industry and other occupations and temporarily may be away from
May 27, 1970

their constituency for weeks at a time? Even the proxy system in the bill does not provide for them.
Why should not inmates of jails and penitentiaries vote? Why must we hang on to this nineteenth century attitude of punitive treatment instead of rehabilitation? With respect to this whole area of enlarging the opportunity and convenience for a maximum number of people to vote, I submit that this bill, even with its improvements, is still inadequate and does not measure up to the principles I outlined at the beginning of my address, those principles which should be embodied in the good electoral law of any free and democratic society.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
The bill should not contain provisions discriminating against parties in opposition. I will be frank; I am particularly concerned about second and third parties in opposition. I urge even more strongly that it should not discriminate against new parties or parties presently unrepresented in Parliament. People change, times change and Parliaments change. No Parliament or government has the right to intrude in respect of decisions that should be made only by the voters.
Our provisions respecting election costs and expenditures are inadequate. Both our election law and electoral practices outside the law allow the continuation of money-raising and spending practices that are a hangover of the worst days of the pork-barrel, coercive and perverted conduct of the old line political parties of generations ago. Our electoral process is financed in a manner that stacks the deck in favour of those in power, those who have been established even longer and those who are already wealthy. It stacks the deck against the individual or party that is effectively prevented from acquiring sufficient financial resources to allow, at least, a nearly-equal presentation of alternative candidates and policies. A commission report on election expenses gathers dust. It contains the basis for real reform. It must be acted upon before the next general election. I submit that in this area more than in any other we find the cause of most of the disgust and dissatisfaction on the part of the public of Canada and on the part of reputable politicians.
I am trying to restrain myself from being too partisan. I do not suppose I shall succeed 100 per cent. I credit the present members of the House for having far better political motives, in terms of their determination to implement
Canada Elections Act
the democratic process, than did those who sat here in previous decades. But I still sense reluctance in some places with respect to the full disclosure of political party finances, the source of those finances and where the money is spent. There is still some reluctance to disclose the financing of something that ought to be public's business.
The further inadequacies in the act-I am talking of discrimination-are the result of an old hangover from pork-barrel days. The appointment of returning officers by Governor in Council gives an unfair advantage to the party in power, no matter which party it may be. It detracts from the impartiality of the officer and makes the returning officer subject to suspicion. It is unfair to him and I submit it is also unfair to the Chief Electoral Officer. Including a candidate's party affiliation on the ballot is an improvement in the law, but that provision is not completely in accord with the principle that we must not discriminate against minor or new parties or in favour of the established, larger parties. No government or Parliament has the right to introduce unreasonable prohibitions which would prevent minor or new parties being recognized. There must be no unreasonable prohibitions with respect to a candidate's political affiliation being included on the ballot.
The provision in the bill requiring 75 candidates to be nominated by the twenty-eighth day before polling day, although nominations in 253 ridings do not close until the twenty-first day before polling day, obviously constitutes a serious conflict in the bill. But more serious than that is the requirement with respect to 75 candidates: If that figure is not met by a party, its status as a registered party is withdrawn and the name of the party will not be mentioned on the ballots. The Standing Committee recommended that to constitute a party you should have candidates running in 10 per cent of 264 constituencies, or that to have 26 or 27 candidates running would qualify a party for registration and inclusion of political affiliation on the ballots. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) and the cabinet may feel that this figure is too low. I assure the government that this matter was discussed thoroughly by the members of the committee. The discussion was non-partisan. Even if the committee's decision was not unanimous, a great majority of committee members agreed on this point.
I think it is fair to say that most if not all members of the committee felt that access to

the bill to be good. It was certainly a good move to combine them so they could be found in one place.
In conclusion I say to the minister in as friendly and happy a manner as I can that I hope that during the debate on this bill he will wear a cap different from the one he wore during the debate on the rule changes. I think most, if not all, members of this House will want to keep the debate as non-partisan as possible. We are all anxious to make whatever contribution we can to ensure good and proper election laws and to improve even further the bill before us. I hope the minister will sympathetically receive ideas and amendments. I hope he will discuss them rationally and objectively without worrying whether some candidate, party or region may obtain a temporary or imaginary advantage. I trust he will be as anxious as the rest of us to improve the bill and enlarge even further the democratic process in our country.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE AND REVISE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my duty and privilege to take part in this debate on the motion for second reading of bill C-215, designed to provide Canada with a modern elections act, adapted to its institutions, and to promote greater and more active democracy.
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I wish to make a few remarks and to take this opportunity to call the attention of the House to the dedication of the chief electoral officer, Mr. Hamel, and to the wonderful manner in which he discharges his duties. As a third party, our group had on several occasions to contact the chief electoral officer in order to make sure that our democratic rights would be safeguarded to the same extent as those of the so-called national parties, the big parties. Now, on every occasion, in a democratic and objective way, he made it a point to co-operate with us, not in order to give us more than to the others, but to protect our rights as much as those of the others. We are proud of him and I want to say here that he may be assured of our co-operation and of our appreciation of his work.
I am glad to mention that the chief electoral officer is a citizen of the Lotbiniere constituency. It is perhaps for this reason that he is an excellent chief electoral officer, and that the electors of the constituency have naturally elected a Creditiste candidate. I would not like to sound parochial, but it seems to me that there are a lot of good people in that constituency.
Canada Elections Act
As to bill C-215, I believe that the election of members is perhaps the most important thing in Canada, a democratic country. Indeed, Parliament is the highest institution in this country. It enacts laws, determines penalties, rules on administrative matters, levies taxes and collects them, distributes family allowances, old age security pensions, and so on.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, Parliament is more or less the cornerstone of the much-vaunted democracy.
Now, in order to elect members who will truly reflect the will of the people on whose behalf they wish to govern, there must be a link between this supreme institution, Parliament, and the people. This link is none other than the electoral legislation and to the extent that the electoral law of a country protects the interests of its citizens, Parliament will truly reflect the will of the people. When the electoral legislation tends to protect the individual and the petty interests of a particular political party, when it condones fraud or is not precise enough, many complications are bound to crop up and the election of representatives may not truly reflect the will of the people.
That is why, on reading the major amendments to be made to the Elections Act, we feel very happy. In fact, the proposed amendments not only will ensure the secrecy of the vote but also its effectiveness.
An elections act has important objects. I shall mention first of all the effectiveness of enumeration. When this is done in an efficient and honest way, preliminary and official lists are consisted with the number of franchised electors. To the extent that the enumeration is well done, the voting lists will be accurate. In this way, everything is above board.
It has been proved on several occasions that enumeration and the appointment of enumerators are tainted with partisanship. In the past, enumeration was done more or less honestly and accurately. One should not be surprised to note that several electors entitled to vote were denied that right.
I personally knew of people from a whole street block who were not enumerated because of two scheming enumerators and, at the time, the third parties were hard hit because they did not have their say.
In that regard, I feel that the federal Elections Act is sound legislation, as compared to the Quebec legislation which prevents the elector from defending himself, while under

May 27, 1970
Canada Elections Act
the federal legislation, the elector who has not been enumerated may have certain recourses.
Here is what pleases me most perhaps: a person who has not been enumerated can, even though he has not received his notice of enumeration, go to the polling station to cast his vote.
Having said this, at the beginning of the debate I listened with interest to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) who said that a permanent list of voters offered several disadvantages. Indeed, in view of what has happened in other countries, it might not be desirable to adopt a permanent list of voters in Canada. He said that it might cost some $13 million and that, consequently, it was too expensive. He then, dismissed that possibility offhand.
I agree with the President of the Privy Council about the experiment conducted in this regard in other countries.
However, I am still convinced that this is not a reason to maintain the statu quo and refuse to budge.
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed my intention to introduce, at the report stage an amendment to make it compulsory to carry an identity card. Perhaps, at first blush, the necessity of it is not too obvious, but I will try to explain.
Since a permanent voters' list does not perhaps meet best the needs of the Canadian voters, the annual checking of an identity card duly approved by the Governor in Council could certainly stop many abuses at the polls.
Arguing that it would be too expensive and that the experience of other countries has shown that it would not meet our needs, the government rejects the idea of a permanent voting list.
I would like to ask the President of the Queen's Privy Council to allow in the course of the discussion of this bill-and I know that with his experience the chief electoral officer would certainly have interesting proposals to submit in connection with that-the setting up of a permanent list, at least of a system which would enable all Canadians to exercise their franchise without losing between two elections their vested privileges. We must not only make sure that all electors exercise their right to vote, but also prevent any fraud in the exercise of this right. If, in the opinion of the President of the Privy Council, it is not desirable to establish a permanent list in

order to ensure that each voter be able to exercise his voting rights, something should be done, at the very least, to avoid fraud.
There are therefore two major goals to achieve and it seems to me that the government is shilly-shallying and does not seem willing to take all possible action to ensure the integrity of the voting process.
That is why I intend to move an amendment in due time in order to make it compulsory to carry an identity card, so that whenever the voter goes to the poll to exercise his franchise, he would have to show his card to the clerks or to the representatives of the various parties. If he is unable to show his card, he then should sign an affidavit or take an oath under the provisions of section 39 of the bill.
Mr. Speaker, I am thinking of many cases that prove that in all the electoral districts of Canada, human nature being what it is, many frauds may be perpetrated where there is no identity card. Up to now, I have taken part in several federal elections either as a candidate or as an organizer, and I found that a number of people cast their vote under another name than their own, thus depriving other citizens from exercising their right to vote.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
This is why I feel that it is an important question to which I will come back in due course, but I am referring to it now, hoping that the President of the Privy Council, who is well-known for his broadness of mind, will consider the possibility of including that provision in the Elections Act. Thus, each Canadian voter would have a card bearing his picture and his signature and he would show it at the polling station. Naturally, it could also serve many other purposes.
To extend the right to vote to the 18-year old group and at the same time to deprive them from protection against fraud, would be to imitate the lobster who, we are told, takes one step forward and two backward. This illusory maturity line is finally done away with in section 14 and I vociferously applaud this long-awaited measure which now lowers the voting age to 18.
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, our democratic and parliamentary institutions will be rejuvenated by the young people entering the political arena. I am not saying that their elders are not as good, but the presence of youth will force the middle-aged people to get out of the rut and closer to the grass-roots instead of being entirely obsessed with protecting their
May 27, 1970

public image. It is not that older people are less competent, but they will have the advantage of no longer being crushed by the Establishment.
This rebirth, due to the lowering of the voting age to 18 will give new life to our parliamentary institutions, which is a matter for rejoicing. I sincerely wish that lowering the voting age to 18 will produce a growing number of dynamic members who will consider their role in the House more important than the political party to which they belong.
In time, political mores will be renewed, the parliamentary institutions will be rejuvenated and adapted to new conditions thanks to the co-operation of middle-aged people and younger men without experience, but dynamic.
Democracy being our most valuable asset, it is imperative that all strata of society-even the young-be allowed to take part in it. Passing an elections act will not do it-unless quite indirectly-but it seems to me that women and young people should gain more say in our institutions.
Since democracy is our most precious possession, the Canadian people should trust their democratic institutions and be able to freely express themselves and to fully exercise their franchise; besides, strict measures should be taken against fraud.
From my humble point of view, this is an essential condition if we want our elections act and our democracy to be more than an illusion.
Mr. Speaker, our people must have faith in their democratic institutions, and an elections act can provide such confidence if it is well drafted. I consider that Bill C-215 can achieve those objectives and I am pleased to tell the House that I will gladly support it.
Mr. Speaker, one must respect the individual and protect its prerogatives and its right to vote. This is why I believe that to reach the goals which I have mentioned, making it compulsory to carry the identity card would surely be a welcome move and would give the population greater faith in our institutions.
The amendments in clause 4 of the bill state that where, by reason of some emergency, it has been necessary to suspend voting at any polling station on the ordinary polling day, the Chief Electoral Officer is empowered to extend the hours of voting at the polling station after the hour fixed for the closing of the poll.
Canada Elections Act
Clause 4(4) should say more specifically how long the polling stations will be closed. If no time limit is set, it may be that the results of the vote will be known only two days after the election.
We should therefore set a time limit in clause 4(4), so that we might, within the shortest delay, solve a problem that could crop up at that time.
If no limit is provided for, we could then know how the vote went only two days after the election. This happened in Warwick at the last provincial election. A polling station was ordered closed and the results were known only the following morning. Such a situation was caused by someone at a polling station.
A time limit should be set so as to give more authority if possible to the officers in charge and to the chief electoral officer.
There is another point I must raise. Indeed, under clauses 1 and 3 of clause 14, the right to vote is granted to 18-year-olds, and it is stated that Canadian citizens only will be qualified as electors. It is also stated that every British subject, other than a Canadian citizen, who was qualified as an elector on the 25 day of June, 1968, and has not, since that date, ceased to be ordinarily resident in Canada, is deemed to be qualified as an elector.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain), if the right to vote is granted at 18, I think we should very soon consider setting the legal age at 18 in every field.
I shall quote examples which will seem rather funny to my hon. colleagues. In the province of Quebec, if someone under 21 wishes to get married, he must ask his parents for their written consent.
I cannot very well imagine a Creditiste member and his prospective bride, both 19 years of age, having to seek their respective fathers' consent to get married.
If those young people were unfortunate enough to have a staunch Progressive Conservative father and an adamantly Liberal mother, they might never be able to get married since they would never obtain leave to do so.
It is certainly timely now to lower the legal age from 21 to 18 not only where the federal elections act is concerned but at every level.
I will now give another example of a problem which is bound to arise. Let us suppose that a 19 year old citizen is elected as a member of Parliament. He may be invited to

May 27, 1370
Canada Elections Act
a cocktail party at a hotel. If he is invited in Ontario or in Quebec either he will be prohibited from setting foot in the hotel or he will not be allowed to have a drink with his guests, and this, because he is not yet 21 years old.
There is some truth in these examples and we should certainly make 18 years the legal age in every case.
If at 18 someone can be a fullfledged citizen, cast his vote and be elected to the House, we should, I think, make that age uniform. The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres was probably right in emphasizing his concern in this respect.
There is another clause to which I would like to draw the attention of the House and that is clause 16. It says that the residence of a person who wishes to qualify as an elector will be considered as of the first day of the enumeration date rather than as of the day the brief is issued.
The clause referred to is clause 16, in Bill C-125. I would like to commend those who drafted this clause of the bill which further enhances the possibilities for the voters to get their names on the lists of electors.
To my mind, the limit formerly in effect was unacceptable.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, the provisions of clause 16 please me, and I think those of sub-clause 20 of clause 18 are excellent. They can be summed up as follows: an elector who has been enumerated and whose name does not appear on the preliminary list of electors can obtain a voting certificate without producing the notice of enumeration.
Here, I should like to relate a personal experience to prove to my hon. colleagues the importance of this section. During the last provincial election, in the riding of Lot-biniere, at Sainte-Croix, Sainte-Antoine-de-Tilly, Joly and Val-Alain, the names of over 120 persons had been listed on the preliminary list. The revising officers went around and took it upon themselves to remove the names of those 120 persons from those lists.
They reported to the county's returning officer without advising the people concerned, so that a few days before election day, those people, whose names appeared on the preliminary list, no longer had the right to vote. And the Provincial Elections Act provides that in the absence of complaints on the part of an elector whose name is deleted from the list, 
that same elector cannot by any means exercise his franchise. By allowing an elector to vote just the same without having his notice of enumeration, clause 18 is already an improvement fraud. Suppose some electors are willing to vote for a minor party, either the New Democratic party or the Ralliement cre-ditiste, and that one revising officer is Progressive Conservative and the other a Liberal, they might connive with each other to delete those electors' names from the lists without telling them, and those electors would then be helpless.
I wonder where the democratic right comes in. That is why I am happy to see clause 18, but it seems to me that it does not go far enough.
I should like to come back to section 13, which may be summarized as follows: The political parties wishing to support candidates in a federal election in Canada will have to file an application with the Chief Electoral Officer. I agree as far as that.
Moreover, the same clause provides that any new party wishing to have its name entered on the voting ballots must have candidates in at least 75 of the electoral districts of Canada on the twenty-eighth day before polling day.
Like the hon. member for Regina Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin), I want to say that I completely disagree with the second part of clause 13. The number of 75 set by the government means that it is up to the government to impose its definition of a national party.
The Ralliement creditiste was the first in this House to ensure the presence and to defend the democratic rights of a group of men who are neither Liberals nor Progressive Conservatives. It is not the responsibility of the government, in my opinion, to set up a minimum number of 75 candidates to ensure the recognition of a party. It seems to me that in such a case, the government shows discrimination against people who wish to elect a group of men who could do as efficient a job as any member of any other party.
Therefore, I should like to call the attention of the President of the Privy Council to clause 13 asking him to remove in the second part only, the figure of 75 and to replace it with the phrase: "a minimum of 10 to 20 per cent," as was suggested by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre. Then it seems to me that the government would show its broadmindedness and that it would not close the
May 27, 197C

door of Parliament to the people. Mr. Speaker, we must be more broadminded.
The summary of the amendment mentions under clause 46: proxy voting-and this is an important part of Bill C-215-that can only be used on the ordinary polling day is instituted for fishermen, marines, prospectors, full-time students, who are performing their usual duties or pursuing their studies, are away from their usual place of residence on the advance polling day or ordinary polling day, as well as people who, due to illness or physical incapacity, are unable to go to the poll.
Mr. Speaker, proxy voting is an improvement over the former elections act. However, it is obvious that this system should be explained fully in simple terms so that voters whether educated or not are able to understand it fully and make use of it. It seems to me that this clause is worthy of support, because this is something both new and better.
I would like to mention, as an example, the Frontenac riding, which, as everybody knows, has no representative at the present time. Mr. Speaker, our present Elections Act has a deficiency which should be looked into immediately. As a matter of fact, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) should be required to call a by-election in a riding where there is a vacancy within three months after the beginning of the vacancy.
Mr. Speaker, a riding such as that of Frontenac, like any other in Canada, has the right to be represented in the House and it should not be left to one man to decide, after six months or a year, whether that riding shall have a representative or not. It seems to me that such a practice is discriminatory and that as long as it is allowed under our Elections Act, the population will not have confidence in our democratic institutions.
This is all the more true as the people are entitled to be represented in the House. There should be incorporated in the Elections Act a specific provision stipulating that within three months following a vacancy in a constituency, the prime minister must order a by-election. Thus, the democratic rights of people concerned would be respected.
And on behalf of the electors of the Frontenac constituency, which is close to mine, I insist on the government calling a by-election as soon as possible. The people there need to elect once again a Creditiste to represent them in the House, and they are eager to be able to do so.
Canada Elections Act
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-215 is an improvement but it will remain quite limited as long as the financing of our political parties is not put in order.
Mr. Speaker, whatever elections act we pass, however honest the provisions designed to prevent any fraud may be, the citizens' democratic rights will not be safeguarded unless specific measures are adopted in order to protect the decision of the people and to prevent money from being the prime factor in democracy.
If one believes in democracy and wants to live up to it, what is most important is the will of the people and not the undue influence of money.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
If we refuse to pursue an ostrich policy, if we are sincere and straight-forward, we must admit that in politics, both in Canada and in the United States and in other countries, money has always been the determining factor of a man's success. It is money which today elects our rulers, our political parties and our members of Parliament, regardless of their competence, their ideas or their objectives. Money is all-powerful. The richest is the strongest. So long as the financing of political parties is not put in order and their expenses are not checked, our elections act and our institutions will remain a farce, because in the end, it is still and always money which sends our members to Parliament. It is money which elects them, which influences them at election time, and which decides afterwards whether they will be reelected or not, according as they have served or not the interests of finance.
Bill C-215 is a fundamental bill. It tends to modernize the Elections Act in order to give the Canadian people a little more faith in our parliamentary democratic institutions. But it is only a drop in the ocean. Until something is done to implement the studies which have been made and are gathering dust on the shelves, the electors will be the losers. Earlier the President of the Privy Council said that these things will perhaps be discussed early next fall, that is in a year from now.
Now that we are about to pass Bill C-215 which tends to modernize our parliamentary democratic institutions, I would like the President of the Privy Council to assure us that the report of the committee inquiring into election expenditures will not remain a dead letter. I say and I repeat that until we overcome the problem of money in politics, until

May 27, 1970
Canada Elections Act
we give the same rights to all political parties insofar as money is concerned, as long as the candidates of the various political parties are enslaved by money during election campaigns and as long as governments kowtow to finance, democracy will only be a farce.
There are perhaps many young people and older people too who believe less and less in democracy, because they know as well as I do that money is the master in politics. That is why I can only urge that specific regulations be enacted with regard to the expenses incurred and authorized by political parties during an election campaign.
Before I close my remarks, I again urge my colleagues to consider seriously the possibility of amending Bill C-215 in order to make it compulsory to carry the identity card. Then we will have shown our intention to avoid as many fraudulent acts as possible when using our franchise, this being an essential right in any democratic society.
There, Mr. Speaker, we wish the adoption of the bill under study, and soon afterwards, the adoption of another bill for the control of electoral spending, in order that the hon. members really be true servants of the people and not of Mammon.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE AND REVISE
speechtext:
It
would be wrong of me, Mr. Speaker, not to speak, at least for a few minutes, during consideration of the motion on the second reading of the bill amending the Elections Act, were it only to thank very sincerely my colleagues who sat on the committee responsible for the consideration of the bill and who a while ago made some quite flattering remarks about me.
I would like, however, as chairman of the committee responsible for the amendment of this legislation, to put on record the fact that during the few months during which we worked together, we have truly attained that essential kind of discussion which excludes any partisanship and I think that we have worked harmoniously together, so that almost all our decisions were unanimous. I believe that this reflects favourably on the report which together we have drawn and tabled in the House just before the drafting of the bill by the legal officers of the Crown.
As someone just said and as it was repeated this afternoon, the Elections Act does provide an extremely important democratic mechanism. It is all the more so that, if we compare it with that of electoral legislation in

other countries, we conclude that the proposed electoral system is as good if not better than that of all other democratic countries where permanent electoral rolls have been established and voting made mandatory. Generally speaking, it can be said that implementation of the proposed Canadian electoral legislation will, I think, make our electoral machinery one of the best that can exist in democratic countries.
As for the various amendments that have been considered, I would like to express my personal feelings. I will deal particularly with the fact of allowing the 18-year-olds to vote. Before doing so, I want to talk about an interview I watched on the French television network of CBC. Some negative questions were put to the chief electoral officer; he was asked why the idea of having a permanent voting list had been given up.
I am alluding to the speech of the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin). If he had taken part in the committee proceedings, he might have understood why on two occasions, we studied the opportunity of establishing a permanent voters' list. The committee rejected the proposal for various reasons, which had little to do with the reasons that were brought forward this afternoon.
It was not sufficiently emphasized that the committee refused to consider favourably the setting up of a permanent list on account of the high cost of such an endeavour which is estimated at $13 million a year. Besides, due to the shortcomings of our present democratic system, two factors combined make it impossible to prepare an absolutely effective permanent list.
The members of the committee were gainst an expenditure of 13 million a year in view of the fact that despite this outlay of money the list would not achieve all the objectives intended.
The great mobility of our population has also motivated the decision of committee members. As a matter of fact, according to statistics, 25 per cent of the population move every four years. Considering also that elections are not held at set dates and that it is up to the Prime Minister alone to set the date, a permanent electoral list would not be efficient.
In fact, the enumeration would have to be done over every six months because of the mobility of the people. The committee mem-
May 27. 1970

bers have also concluded that such a permanent list, while attempting to deprive as few electors as possible of their right to vote, would have the very opposite effect.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
This list, which after all would cost 13 million dollars, to be of any use, would have to be adhered to without the necessity of frequent revisions. Therefore, the factors I mentioned, i.e., the mobility of our population, the prime minister's prerogative to call an election, and never at any fixed date, added to the annual expense of 13 million dollars, and our concern with depriving as few voters as possible of the exercise of their rights have resulted in failure to achieve the objective we sought.
Elimination of the principle of a permanent election list on grounds of inefficiency rather than of cost, however heavy, involves eliminating a system of absentee voting, which is only conceivable if there is a permanent list.
But the permanent list being eliminated and the absentee voting system having gone overboard, since it was essentially predicated upon a permanent list, other means had to be found. But which means? The setting up of a system depriving the least possible number of citizens of their right to vote, an extension of the structures, so as to make the former rules easier and more flexible. Voters who went to the polls would be deemed to ordinarily reside in the electoral district in which they lived on the enumeration date, and this is another improvement.
We have also considered a revision system of electoral lists which would make the rules more flexible and remove the possibilities of clerical errors in the setting up of the electoral list.
We further considered a way to make it easier for the voter to exercise his franchise in such a way that he would not have to inscribe only a crossmark or an "X" as was the case in the past, and to lower the voting age from 21 to 18.
If we analyze the whole legislation, we have to come to the conclusion that in spite of its defects, it has reached the main objectives that we had in mind, that is to say to reach the greatest number possible of voters, for the reasons I have set out, discarding thus the principle of a permanent list of voters which would have, as the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) pointed out, made easier an absentee voting system, fraught with difficulties and shortcomings.
Canada Elections Act
Mr. Speaker, the question of proxy vote was also dealt with. It does not equally apply to all social strata,-we realize that-because if according to the principles of democracy, we wish to extend the franchise to the greatest possible number of people, we should understand however that the voter, even when rather apathetic, will try to take part in a democratic electoral system and do his best to exercise his right to vote. By changing the provisions of the act concerning temporary polling stations, by making voting by proxy more convenient for the voters, there is a distinct improvement. In fact when the majority of the people wish to change government, there is always a possibility that a small number of voters do not exercise their franchise through carelessness, negligence or lack of interest rather than inability.
I am coming back now to a major provision of the bill concerning the lowering of the voting age to 18.
If I am not mistaken, everyone has said that this was an improvement. I can conceive that this is an improvement, perhaps a major one, because another 10 per cent at least of the voters, who are among the youngest members of society, will be allowed to vote. This imposes upon political parties a heavy responsibility which is basic in my opinion.
Unless I am totally misinformed I submit that none of the federal political parties is sufficiently structured to communicate and dialogue with the young people of 14, 15 and 16 who will have the right to vote come the next general election.
This means, if we are to analyze quite objectively the social impact of the amendments to the act on the Canadian electorate as a whole, that at the time of an election, the children of 14 will be those who, at the next election, will be in a position to overthrow the government from which they will be far removed, due to their school or other activities, if some machinery has not been set up.
There is a potential danger there-and the people will have to get used to it. Parliament must set up the necessary machinery so that it can communicate with the young while respecting their yearning for objectivity and making allowance for their readiness to defend ideals which are not always commendable and are more often than not negative rather than positive, as experience has shown. Young people have, indeed, generally adopted a negative rather than a positive approach; they have dedicated themselves to the quest of ideals basically opposed to their

May 27, 1970
Canada Elections Act
primary interests. This means that in a well organized democracy-and I emphasize the fact-this idea will have to be accepted as such. Some deans or professors will also have to be in a position to influence the youths of 14, 15 and 16 who might be called upon to vote in the next election. We shall have to provide the political parties, through their representatives or otherwise, with some kind of means of reaching the young people in our high schools, and in the other places they haunt, in order to talk to them so that they are not just geared to some kind of idealism, often very far removed, from reality, but to reality itself.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
My remarks stem from what has been the case in Quebec where he voting age was lowered to 18 years for the last election. In that province, between 60 and 75 per cent of the young people got enthusiastic over a political philosophy. But, when four political parties are competing in an election, and when it is realized that a huge majority of a certain sector of the population, namely the young people, vote in favour of a certain party, that is something dangerous, if we do not devise new structures so that the young might be informed about public administration at both the provincial and the federal levels.
Provided that objective is reached, 10 per cent of the young people, that is perhaps the best element of the population, through their usual dynamism, and their normal eagerness in their search for the truth, will contribute to our society. Thanks to that mechanism, our electoral mores can be purged.
Members of all political parties should dialogue with the young, instead of leading them to seek ideals which are not always praiseworthy. Let them instil ideals in the young people of 14, 15, and 16 years of age, and set objectives in their best interest and those of the Canadian people as a whole: then we can lay claim to having improved something.
I feel that, in the analysis of the revision of the Elections Act, which delves deeply into several sectors, particularly where the vote by proxy is concerned, which applies especially to students, we should allow the students to vote in their respective ridings, where they are known, for the very good reason that
they should not be deprived of their franchise because their functions, their work, demand that they attend a university, very often far away from their usual residence or that of their parents.
On the whole, an analysis of the bill reveals that its objects are those that I listed very briefly a while ago. Compared to earlier amendments to the act, and considering the extent of some of the present amendments, the government should, of necessity, enable the chief electoral officer to dispose of far more funds than he has now, to inform the people through the normal media, namely television, radio and newspapers, so that they might, long before elections are held, be better informed about the new election machinery that will be in force in the future.
For that purpose, the Chief Electoral Officer needs additional funds and much greater freedom, and he has neither at the present time.
The pros and cons of the amendments were pointed out a few moments ago. I will say it again: all the committee members who studied this bill really tried to be objective and to find the best possible means of providing the Canadian people as a whole with an election apparatus that would be every bit as good as in other countries.
In conclusion, I will just point to the hon. member for Lotbiniere, who demanded that the law be amended to allow for a by-election in the Frontenac constituency that such an amendment should be made rather to the House of Commons Act, which gives the Prune Minister a six month-time-limit, which may seem very long to order the holding of an election. Should the House of Commons Act ever be revised, that would be the time to make suggestions.
Such are, Mr. Speaker, the few comments I wanted to make.

subtopic: SUMMARY OF THE MAIN AMENDMENTS MADE TO THE CANADA ELECTIONS ACT (REFERENCES IN BRACKETS ARE TO PERTINENT SECTIONS OF BILL C-215)

speechtext:
1.	The French terminology suggested by the Staff of the Statute Revision Commission is adopted.
2.	The duties and responsibilities which, under the Canada Elections Act, as amended, are at present assigned to the Representation Commissioner are transferred back to the Chief Electoral Officer (Sec. 4(2) and (3), Sec. 61(1) and Sec. 70).
3.	Any reference to a specific salary to be paid to the Chief Electoral Officer is deleted from the Act and, instead, his salary is equated to that of a puisne judge of the Exchequer Court of Canada, including any additional salary authorized by section 20 of the Judges Act (Sec. 3(4)).
4.	Where, by reason of some emergency, it has been necessary to suspend voting at any polling station on the ordinary polling day, the Chief Electoral Officer is empowered to extend the hours of voting at the polling station after the hour fixed for the closing of the poll (Sec. 4(4)).
5.	Failure on the part of a returning officer to revise his polling division boundaries as instructed by the Chief Electoral Officer is a cause for removal from office (Sec. 7(3)(f)).
6.	A vacancy in the office of returning officer will be filled within 60 days from the date on which the Chief Electoral Officer has been informed of the vacancy (Sec. 7(5)).
7.	Returning officers in electoral districts specified in Schedule III are allowed to appoint additional election clerks on the authorization of the Chief Electoral Officer (Sec. 8(10), (11) and (12)).
8.	Polling division boundaries will be established to include approximately 250 electors, or a multiple thereof, per polling division (Sec. 10(2) and (3)).
9.	The Chief Electoral Officer is given the power, when requested not later than the date of the issue of the writ, to declare built up areas abutting incoporated towns and
cities of 5,000 population or more urban polling divisions, if he deems it expedient (Sec. 11(3)).
10.	The Chief Electoral Officer is given the power, when requested not later than the date of the issue of the writ, to declare areas within incorporated towns and cities of 5,000 population or more rural polling divisions, if he deems it expedient (Sec. 11(4)).
11.	Voting age is reduced to eighteen and only Canadian citizens are qualified as electors (British subjects, other than Canadian citizens, who were qualified as electors on the 25th day of June, 1968, and have not ceased since that date to be ordinarily resident in Canada, are deemed to be qualified as electors) (Sec. 14(1) to (3)).
12.	The residence requirement to be qualified to vote will be determined as of the first day of enumeration, instead of as of the date of the issue of the writ (Sec. 16).
13.	Ministers, priests and teachers who change the place of their ordinary residence from one polling division to another between the first day of enumeration and polling day, will be allowed to have their names entered on the list of electors for the polling division to which they have moved, even if such polling division is in the same electoral district (Sec. 17(9)).
14.	The privilege accorded ministers, priests and teachers is extended to persons seasonally employed in the fishing industry, other than fishermen (Sec. 17(9)(c)).
15.	The distinction between persons temporarily engaged in public works and those in non-public works is abolished (Sec. 17(12) and (13)).
16.	A candidate who was a member of Parliament on the day before the dissolution of Parliament immediately preceding the election, is entitled to vote in the electoral district where he is a candidate; this right is extended to his spouse and dependants (Sec. 17(16)).

May 27, 1970
17.	The procedures for appointing urban enumerators, revising agents and substitute revising officers are clarified and their duties and responsibilities clearly defined (Sec. 18, Sched. A, Rules (4), (27) and (68)).
18.	The returning officer and revising officer are nermitted to correct clerical errors made by the enumerators or the printers in the preparation of the preliminary lists of electors (Sec. 18(4) and Sec. 18, Sched. A, Rules (42) and (43)).
19.	At the request of the returning officer, the revising officer will be allowed to rectify mistakes made by the enumerators or revising agents (Sec. 18, Sched. A, rules (41) and (80)).
20.	An elector who has been enumerated but whose name has been left off the preliminary list of electors may obtain a certificate to vote without producing his enumeration notice in Form No. 7 (Sec. 18(2)).
21.	With the prior approval of the Chief Electoral Officer and for good and valid reason, a returning officer will be authorized to amalgamate two or more polling divisions (Sec. 18(29) and (30)).
22.	Only postmasters of post offices in the urban areas of an electoral district will receive a notice of revision (Sec. 18, Sched. A, Rule (34)).
23.	The days for the sittings for revising the preliminary lists of electors, in both urban and rural areas, are advanced by one day (Sec. 18, Sched. A, Rule (39) and Sched. B, Rule (13)).
24.	Revising officers are authorized to take names off the preliminary lists of electors at the request of the persons themselves who want their names to be removed from the lists (Sec. 18, Sched. A, Rule (42)).
25.	Revising agents are authorized to accept statements from relatives by blood or marriage (Sec. 18, Sched. A Rule (76(b)).
26.	The number of copies of the statements of changes and additions supplied to candidates is reduced from five to three (Sec. 18, Sched. A, Rules (63) and (64)).
27.	The proclamation will be printed in both official languages in every electoral district in Canada (Sec. 19(1)).
28.	The procedure for the nomination of candidates is set out separately from the
provisions dealing with polling day and nomination day, and is precisely set out (Sections 22 and 23).
29.	Political parties in Canada wishing to endorse candidates at an election for the House of Commons will have to register with the Chief Electoral Officer; in addition, any new party that wishes to be identified on the ballot papers must have candidates officially nominated in 75 electoral districts in Canada on the 28th day before polling day (Section 13).
30.	The age to be a candidate is reduced from 21 to 18 (Sec. 20).
31.	Persons who are specifically disqualified from voting are ineligible as candidates (Sec. 21(l)(h)).
32.	Persons who consent to be candidates at an election knowing that they are ineligible will be guilty of an offence (Sec. 21(4)).
33.	Returning officers will be permitted to centralize up to ten polling stations and, whenever possible, shall locate their polling stations in schools or other public buildings (Sec. 33 (6) and (9)).
34.	The rights and obligations of candidates and their agents in polling stations are clarified and more precisely set out (Sec. 36).
35.	The Friday immediately preceding polling day, instead of Saturday, will be the last day for receiving applications for transfer certificates (Sec. 43(1)).
36.	The procedure for voting is clarified and precisely set out (Sec. 45).
37.	Anyone who records the serial number of a ballot paper is guilty of an offence (Sec. 45(10)).
38.	Where an elector is unable to mark his ballot for any reason, a friend or relative accompanying him will be permitted to mark the ballot on his behalf (Sec. 45(14) to (18)).
39.	A system of proxy voting, exercisable only on the ordinary polling day, is instituted for fishermen, mariners, prospectors and fulltime students who, in the normal course of their employment or studies as such, are absent from their place of ordinary residence on advance polling day and ordinary polling day, as well as for persons who, through illness or physical incapacity, are unable to attend and vote at a polling station (Sec. 46).﻿May 27, 1970

40.	The proxy provisions relating to fulltime students are in lieu of their prior entitlement to be on two lists.
41.	The format of the ballot paper is changed to contain a small circular space at the right of and completely separated from the space where the name of the candidate is printed, in which space the elector will indicate his choice (Sec. 31(2) and Form No. 37);
The Chief Electoral Officer is required to prepare a new design for the back of the ballot paper (Sec. 116).
42.	The political affiliation of a candidate who is endorsed by the leader of a registered party or his designated representative will be printed on the ballot paper (Sec. 31(1) (b)).
43.	The requirement to indicate the address and occupation of a candidate on the ballot paper is deleted.
44.	A ballot paper will not be rejected solely because it was marked with a writing instrument other than a black lead pencil or with a mark other than a cross (Sec. 51(4) (b)).
45.	A returning officer will apply to a judge for a recount if, on the official addition of the votes, there is an equality of votes between two or more candidates and an additional vote for one of such candidates would entitle him to be declared elected (Sec. 53(7)).
46.	When a judicial recount is conducted, the persons who are entitled to attend and the election material to which the judge may refer, are clearly set out in the Act; the judge is entitled to hire clerical assistance and is empowered to summon before him a deputy returning officer or poll clerk, if necessary; the attendance of an election clerk is no longer mandatory; a judge will be permitted to terminate a recount at any time upon request (Sec. 56).
47.	The Chief Electoral Officer is authorized to pay revising agents by warrants, give accountable advances to returning officers and withhold payments to election officers who have failed to carry out their duties (Sec. 61(4), (8) and (16)).
48.	The penalty and offences provisions of the Canada Elections Act are consolidated, whenever possible, and the penalties incorporated into a single section (Sections 65 to 79).
49.	The outlets for the sale of alcoholic beverages are closed on ordinary polling day only while the polls are open (Sec. 67).

50.	A candidate and his official agent are prohibited from providing alcoholic beverages during an election period for election purposes (Sec. 66(3)).
51.	The restriction for paying transportation of electors to the polls is deleted. (Sec. 15(3) (d)).
52.	Any form of tampering with the election material or campaign literature of a candidate is an offence (Sec. 73).
53.	The right to vote at advance polls is extended to persons confined to wheelchairs or otherwise incapacitated and these polls will be located in places providing ease of access to such incapacitated persons (Sections 91(6) and 93).
54.	The notice of advance polls will be published thirty days before polling day, rather than twelve days as in the past (Sec. 92(3)).
55.	It is now an offence to make a premature count of the votes cast at an advance poll (Sec. 95(9)).
56.	The minimum age for all election officers, except returning officers, whose minimum age shall continue to be twenty-one, will be eighteen (Sec. 98(2) and (3)).
57.	Political broadcasts are forbidden only on the ordinary polling day and on the one day immediately preceding it (Sec. 99 (1)).
58.	The provisions relating to premature publication of election results are amended to make it possible to take action against corporations as well as individuals (Sec. 105(2)).
59.	The present provisions of the Canadian Forces Voting Rules are extended to public servants posted abroad and their dependants as well as to dependants of the members of the forces serving abroad and for this purpose, Schedule II of the Canada Elections Act is re-titled "Special Voting Rules" (Sec. 109).
60.	Persons entitled to vote as Veteran electors under the Special Voting Rules are entitled to choose, as their place of ordinary residence, the institution in which they are resident while receiving treatment, provided they have been there for at least one year (Sec. 67(3) (b) of the Special Voting Rules).
61.	A candidate or his accredited representative will be authorized to inspect, in the office of the returning officer, the list of Canadian Forces and Public Service electors, entitled to vote under the Special Voting

May 27. 1970
Buies, who are ordinarily resident of his electoral district and make extracts therefrom (Sections 12(2) and 28(D).
62.	The list of Canadian Forces electors prepared by each commanding officer is no longer open for inspection by candidates or their representatives (Paragraph 29 of the present Canadian Forces Voting Buies).
63.	Nomination day in electoral districts other than those specified in Schedule III will be on the twenty-first day before polling day at a general election, instead of the fourteenth day, and the days and times specified for the doing of anything under the Act or Buies will be advanced to permit the vote under the Special Voting Buies to be announced on the ordinary polling day (Sections 22(5) and 52).
64.	The writs of election for a general election will specify the date on which they are returnable (Form No. 1).
65.	A clear distinction is made between the terms "qualified as elector" or "qualified elector" and "qualified to vote".
